On the Graphical rr-Stirling Numbers of the First Kind for Specific Graph Families

Daniel Yaqubi∗ Address: ∗Department of Computer science, University of Torbat-e Jam, Torbat-e Jam, Iran. Email address: yaqubi@tjamcaas.ac.ir, or daniel_yaqubi@yahoo.es and Madjid Mirzavaziri Address: Department of Pure Mathematics, Faculty of Mathematical Sciences, Ferdowsi University of Mashhad, P. O. Box 1159-91775, Mashhad, Iran. Email address: mirzavaziri@gmail.com
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

This paper investigates the graphical rr-Stirling numbers of the first kind, denoted by [Gk]r\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{G}{k}\right]_{r}, which enumerate partitions of a vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) into kk disjoint cycles such that rr specified vertices occupy distinct blocks. We establish closed-form expressions and recursive identities for fundamental graph families, including Path (PnP_{n}), Cycle (CnC_{n}), Star (SnS_{n}), Wheel (WnW_{n}), and Fan (FnF_{n}) graphs.

A primary focus of this study is the statistical characterization of the cycle distribution. We derive explicit formulas for the mean and variance of these numbers, extracted from the structural properties of the rr-cycle polynomials. These results provide a rigorous measure of the average cycle density and variability across different graph topologies, bridging the gap between algebraic combinatorics and the structural analysis of restricted permutations.

Keywords: Graphical rr-Stirling numbers, rr-cycle polynomials, universal vertices, mean, variance, combinatorial moments.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary:11B73; Secondary:62H10, 05A16.

1. Introduction

The Stirling numbers of the first kind [nk]{n\brack k} are fundamental objects in enumerative combinatorics, counting permutations of an nn-element set with exactly kk disjoint cycles. These numbers play a central role in the study of permutation statistics, algebraic combinatorics, and probability theory [10, 11]. Classical results of Goncharov and Feller established deep connections between Stirling numbers, generating polynomials, and asymptotic normality, leading to a Central Limit Theorem for the number of cycles in random permutations.

An important refinement was introduced by Broder [12], who defined the rr-Stirling numbers of the first kind [nk]r{n\brack k}_{r} by imposing the restriction that the first rr elements must lie in distinct cycles. These restricted Stirling numbers interpolate between classical permutations and more constrained cycle structures, and they have been studied extensively in connection with restricted permutations, algebraic identities, and probabilistic limit laws.

Motivated by the interaction between graph structure and cycle decompositions, Barghi and DeFord [13] introduced the graphical Stirling numbers of the first kind [Gk]{G\brack k} for an arbitrary graph GG. These numbers enumerate partitions of the vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) into kk disjoint cycles supported by the edges of GG, allowing both 11-cycles and 22-cycles. When GG is the complete graph KnK_{n}, the numbers [Gk]{G\brack k} reduce to the classical Stirling numbers of the first kind. The sum ∑k[Gk]\sum_{k}{G\brack k}, called the graphical factorial of GG, counts all cycle covers of GG. Although cycle cover enumeration is computationally difficult in general, explicit formulas and structural results can be obtained for sparse or highly structured graph families.

In this paper, we introduce and study the graphical rr-Stirling numbers of the first kind, denoted [Gk]r{G\brack k}_{r}. These numbers count partitions of V⁡(G)V(G) into kk disjoint cycle blocks subject to the additional constraint that rr specified vertices lie in distinct cycles. This definition simultaneously generalizes Broder’s rr-Stirling numbers and the graphical Stirling numbers of the first kind, providing a unified framework for studying restricted cycle decompositions in graphs and modeling combinatorial situations in which designated vertices must participate in closed paths.

Our first objective is to extend enumerative results for [Gk]{G\brack k} to this rr-restricted setting. We derive explicit formulas, recurrence relations, and rr-cycle polynomials for several fundamental families of graphs, including paths (PnP_{n}), cycles (CnC_{n}), stars (SnS_{n}), wheels (WnW_{n}), and fan graphs (FnF_{n}).

Beyond exact enumeration, we investigate the algebraic properties of graphical rr-Stirling numbers. Building on Harper’s seminal work on the real-rootedness and log-concavity of Stirling polynomials [14], as well as subsequent developments by Liu, Yang, and Zhang [15, 16], we study unimodality, log-concavity, and real-rootedness of the associated rr-cycle polynomials for various graph families. These algebraic properties provide strong structural insight and play a crucial role in probabilistic analysis.

From a probabilistic perspective, classical results of Goncharov [10] and Feller [11] established a Central Limit Theorem for the number of cycles in permutations. More recently, asymptotic normality and related limit laws have been studied for generalized Stirling numbers and graph-based combinatorial statistics [17, 18]. In this work, we extend these ideas to the graphical rr-Stirling setting. Using analytic properties of generating polynomials and moment methods, we derive explicit formulas for the mean and variance of the number of cycles and establish Gaussian limiting behavior for several families of graphs as the number of vertices tends to infinity.

Finally, we examine asymptotic behavior across growing families of graphs and analyze how sparsity, degree distribution, and structural constraints influence both enumerative and probabilistic properties. The paper concludes with several conjectures and open problems concerning asymptotic normality, real-rootedness, and algebraic behavior of graphical rr-Stirling polynomials, suggesting promising directions for future research in graph enumeration, algebraic combinatorics, and probabilistic graph theory.

2. Preliminaries and notation

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a simple graph with vertex set V=[n]V=[n] and edge set EE. A graphical cycle partition of GG into kk blocks is a partition of the vertex set π⁡(G)={C1,C2,…,Ck}\pi(G)=\{C_{1},C_{2},\dots,C_{k}\} such that for each block CiC_{i}, one of the following conditions is satisfied:

  • (i)

    |Ci|=1|C_{i}|=1 (a 11-cycle) or |Ci|=2|C_{i}|=2 (a 22-cycle).

  • (ii)

    If |Ci|>2|C_{i}|>2, the induced subgraph G|CiG|_{C_{i}} is Hamiltonian; that is, it is connected and contains at least one cycle that visits each vertex in CiC_{i} exactly once.

In the case of |Ci|>2|C_{i}|>2, we treat CiC_{i} as a specific oriented Hamiltonian cycle within the induced subgraph. The graphical Stirling number of the first kind, denoted by [Gk]{G\brack k}, represents the total number of such partitions of VV into exactly kk cycles. This definition generalizes the classical Stirling numbers by restricting the cycle formation to the edge set of GG.

Definition 2.1.

Let GG be a graph of order nn. The graphical cycle polynomial 𝒞⁡(G,x)\mathcal{C}(G,x) is the generating function for the graphical cycle partition numbers [Gk]{G\brack k}:

𝒞⁡(G,x)=∑k=1n[Gk]​xk\mathcal{C}(G,x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}{G\brack k}x^{k}
Remark 2.2.

Although both the matching polynomial and the graphical cycle polynomial of the first kind are satisfy linear recurrences on some graphs, they encode fundamentally different combinatorial structures.

Example 2.3.

Let W4W_{4} be the wheel graph of order n=5n=5 defined by the join K1∨C4K_{1}\vee C_{4}, with vertex set V⁡(W4)={v0,1,2,3,4}V(W_{4})=\{v_{0},1,2,3,4\}. Here, v0v_{0} represents the central hub, and the induced subgraph of {1,2,3,4}\{1,2,3,4\} is the cycle C4C_{4}. The graph contains |E⁡(W4)|=8|E(W_{4})|=8 edges and 4 triangles (C3C_{3}).

The graphical Stirling numbers [W4k]{W_{4}\brack k} enumerate partitions of V⁡(W4)V(W_{4}) into kk disjoint cycles supported by the graph structure. The distribution is summarized in Table 1.

The resulting graphical cycle partition vector for W4W_{4} is (8,9,14,8,1)(8,9,14,8,1), defining the cycle polynomial:

𝒞⁡(W4,x)=x5+8​x4+14​x3+9​x2+8​x\mathcal{C}(W_{4},x)=x^{5}+8x^{4}+14x^{3}+9x^{2}+8x

The basic properties and specific formulas for well-known graph families are summarized in Table 2.

3. General Statements and Graph Operations

In this section, we formalize the graph-theoretic operations required to establish our recurrence relations. Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a simple graph of order nn.

  • •

    Vertex Deletion: For a vertex vi∈Vv_{i}\in V, let G−viG-v_{i} denote the subgraph induced by V∖{vi}V\setminus\{v_{i}\}. More generally, for a subset U⊂VU\subset V, G−UG-U denotes the subgraph induced by V∖UV\setminus U.

  • •

    Vertex Attachment (Gluing): Let G+v1uG+_{v_{1}}u denote the graph obtained by adding a vertex u∉Vu\notin V and the edge e=(v1,u)e=(v_{1},u), where v1∈Vv_{1}\in V is the point of attachment.

  • •

    Brooming Operation: Let U={u1,u2,…,um}U=\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{m}\} be a set of mm vertices such that V∩U=∅V\cap U=\emptyset. We define the brooming of GG at v1∈Vv_{1}\in V, denoted by G+v1UG+_{v_{1}}U, as the graph with vertex set V∪UV\cup U and edge set E∪{(v1,ui):1≤i≤m}E\cup\{(v_{1},u_{i}):1\leq i\leq m\}.

Example 3.1.

Let G≅C3G\cong C_{3} be the cycle graph with vertices {v1,v2,v3}\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\}. Figure 2 illustrates the transformation of C3C_{3} under deletion, attachment, and brooming. Original vertices are shaded in blue, while added vertices and edges are highlighted in red.

Lemma 3.2.

Let GG be a simple graph. The graphical Stirling numbers [Gk]{G\brack k} satisfy the following recursive and structural identities:

  1. (1)

    Isolation Shift: Let I⊆V⁡(G)I\subseteq V(G) be a set of mm isolated vertices. For k≥mk\geq m:

    [Gk]=[G−Ik−m]{G\brack k}={G-I\brack k-m}
  2. (2)

    Disjoint Union Convolution: Let GG be the disjoint union of two graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}. Then:

    [G1∪G2k]=∑j=1k−1[G1j]​[G2k−j]{G_{1}\cup G_{2}\brack k}=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}{G_{1}\brack j}{G_{2}\brack k-j}
  3. (3)

    The graphical cycle polynomial of their union is given by the product of their individual polynomials:

    𝒞⁡(G1∪G2,x)=𝒞⁡(G1,x)⋅𝒞⁡(G2,x)\mathcal{C}(G_{1}\cup G_{2},x)=\mathcal{C}(G_{1},x)\cdot\mathcal{C}(G_{2},x)
Proof.

(1) Let I={v∈V⁡(G):deg⁡(v)=0}I=\{v\in V(G):\deg(v)=0\}. By definition, every block in a graphical cycle partition must induce a cycle CℓC_{\ell}. Since vertices in II have no incident edges, they cannot participate in induced cycles of length ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2. Consequently, each vertex v∈Iv\in I must form a trivial 1-cycle (C1C_{1}). Since these mm isolated vertices are necessarily partitioned into mm distinct cycles, the problem reduces to partitioning the remaining vertex set V⁡(G)∖IV(G)\setminus I into k−mk-m induced cycles. This yields the identity [G−Ik−m]{G-I\brack k-m}.

(2) Since G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are disjoint, any subset of V⁡(G1∪G2)V(G_{1}\cup G_{2}) that induces a cycle must be a subset of either V⁡(G1)V(G_{1}) or V⁡(G2)V(G_{2}). Thus, a partition of the union into kk cycles is uniquely determined by the union of a jj-cycle partition of G1G_{1} and a (k−j)(k-j)-cycle partition of G2G_{2}. Summing over all valid jj yields the discrete convolution.

(3) By the definition of the graphical cycle polynomial and the convolution property of the cycle partition numbers for disjoint unions:

𝒞⁡(G1∪G2,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(G_{1}\cup G_{2},x) =∑k[G1∪G2k]​xk\displaystyle=\sum_{k}{G_{1}\cup G_{2}\brack k}x^{k}
=∑k(∑j[G1j]​[G2k−j])​xk\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\left(\sum_{j}{G_{1}\brack j}{G_{2}\brack k-j}\right)x^{k}
=(∑j[G1j]​xj)​(∑m[G2m]​xm)\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{j}{G_{1}\brack j}x^{j}\right)\left(\sum_{m}{G_{2}\brack m}x^{m}\right)
=𝒞⁡(G1,x)⋅𝒞⁡(G2,x)\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}(G_{1},x)\cdot\mathcal{C}(G_{2},x)

This completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 3.3.

Let GG be the disjoint union of components G1,G2,…,GmG_{1},G_{2},\dots,G_{m}. The graphical Stirling numbers satisfy the multinomial convolution:

[Gk]=∑j1+⋯+jm=k(∏i=1m[Giji]){G\brack k}=\sum_{j_{1}+\dots+j_{m}=k}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}{G_{i}\brack j_{i}}\right)

Equivalently, the graphical cycle polynomial 𝒞⁡(G,x)=∑k[Gk]​xk\mathcal{C}(G,x)=\sum_{k}{G\brack k}x^{k} is multiplicative over disjoint components:

𝒞⁡(⋃i=1mGi,x)=∏i=1m𝒞⁡(Gi,x)\mathcal{C}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}G_{i},x\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{C}(G_{i},x)
Lemma 3.4.

Let GG be a simple graph and v∉V⁡(G)v\notin V(G). For any w∈V⁡(G)w\in V(G), let G+wvG+_{w}v be the graph formed by attaching vv to ww via a pendant edge. The graphical cycle partition numbers satisfy:

[G+wvk]=[Gk−1]+[G−wk−1]{G+_{w}v\brack k}={G\brack k-1}+{G-w\brack k-1}
Proof.

Consider the vertex vv in G+wvG+_{w}v. Since vv is a pendant vertex with N⁡(v)={w}N(v)=\{w\}, it can only induce a cycle of length 1 or 2.

  • •

    If vv induces a C1C_{1}, the remaining vertices V⁡(G)V(G) must be partitioned into k−1k-1 cycles. There are [Gk−1]{G\brack k-1} such ways.

  • •

    If vv induces a C2C_{2}, it must be the edge v​wvw. The remaining vertices V⁡(G)∖{w}V(G)\setminus\{w\} must be partitioned into k−1k-1 cycles. This corresponds to the graph G−wG-w, yielding [G−wk−1]{G-w\brack k-1} ways.

Summing these disjoint cases gives the result. ∎

Now, we derive the graphical cycle polynomial for the cycle graph CnC_{n} and PnP_{n}. This derivation utilizes Kaplansky’s First Lemma [God], which provides the combinatorial count for matchings in circular arrangements.

Lemma 3.5 (Kaplansky’s Lemma for Circular Arrangements).

The number of ways to select mm non-adjacent edges from a cycle graph CnC_{n} (equivalent to selecting mm non-consecutive objects from nn objects arranged in a circular fashion) is given by:

nn−m​(n−mm)\frac{n}{n-m}\binom{n-m}{m}

where 0≤m≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq m\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor.

Theorem 3.6.

The graphical cycle polynomial of the path graph PnP_{n} is given by:

𝒞⁡(Pn,x)=∑k=⌈n/2⌉n(kn−k)​xk\mathcal{C}(P_{n},x)=\sum_{k=\lceil n/2\rceil}^{n}\binom{k}{n-k}x^{k}

where the coefficients (kn−k)\binom{k}{n-k} correspond to the number of matchings of size n−kn-k in PnP_{n}.

Proof.

In the path graph PnP_{n}, we have only 1-cycles and 2-cycles. Thus, any graphical cycle partition of V⁡(Pn)V(P_{n}) into kk subsets must consist solely of mm induced C2C_{2} subgraphs (edges) and ss induced C1C_{1} subgraphs (vertices).

The total number of vertices is 2​m+s=n2m+s=n and the total number of cycles is m+s=km+s=k, which implies m=n−km=n-k. According to Kaplansky’s Lemma 3.5, the number of ways to choose jj items from mm items in a row such that no two are consecutive is given by:

[Pnk]=((n−1)−(n−k)+1n−k)=(kn−k)\begin{bmatrix}P_{n}\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\binom{(n-1)-(n-k)+1}{n-k}=\binom{k}{n-k}

Summing over all possible values of kk (where n−k≤kn-k\leq k implies k≥n/2k\geq n/2) yields the result. ∎

Theorem 3.7.

The graphical cycle polynomial of the cycle graph CnC_{n} for n≥3n\geq 3 is given by:

𝒞⁡(Cn,x)=2​x+∑k=⌈n/2⌉n[Cnk]​xk\mathcal{C}(C_{n},x)=2x+\sum_{k=\lceil n/2\rceil}^{n}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{C_n}{k}x^{k}

where the coefficients [Cnk]=nk​(kn−k)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{C_n}{k}=\frac{n}{k}\binom{k}{n-k} for k≥2k\geq 2 correspond to the number of matchings of size n−kn-k in CnC_{n}.

Proof.

By definition, the graphical cycle polynomial 𝒞⁡(G,x)\mathcal{C}(G,x) enumerates the partitions of the vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) into kk disjoint cycles, where a partition into kk cycles contributes to the coefficient of xkx^{k}. For the cycle graph G=CnG=C_{n}, the admissible cycle lengths in a vertex partition are strictly constrained by the graph’s topology.

I. The Case k=1k=1 (Hamiltonian Cycle):

For k=1k=1, the vertex set must be covered by a single cycle of length nn. While CnC_{n} contains exactly one such subgraph, we account for the two possible orientations (clockwise and counter-clockwise) of the Hamiltonian cycle, consistent with the treatment of cycles in directed contexts (analogous to Stirling numbers of the first kind). This yields the term:

2​x1=2​x.2x^{1}=2x.

II. The Case k≥2k\geq 2.

For k≥2k\geq 2, the partition cannot include the Hamiltonian cycle. Furthermore, for n≥3n\geq 3, the cycle graph CnC_{n} does not contain any vertex-disjoint cycles of length 3≤ℓ<n3\leq\ell<n. Consequently, any partition of V⁡(Cn)V(C_{n}) into kk components must consist exclusively of:

  • •

    mm cycles of length 2 (representing a matching of mm disjoint edges),

  • •

    ss cycles of length 1 (representing isolated vertices).

To determine the number of components kk, we consider the following system:

(1) 2​m+s\displaystyle 2m+s =n(Vertex constraint)\displaystyle=n\quad\text{(Vertex constraint)}
(2) m+s\displaystyle m+s =k(Component constraint)\displaystyle=k\quad\text{(Component constraint)}

Solving this system yields m=n−km=n-k. Thus, a vertex partition into kk components is bijectively related to a matching of size n−kn-k in CnC_{n}.

By Kaplansky’s Lemma 3.5 and substituting m=n−km=n-k we have

[Cnk]=nn−(n−k)​(n−(n−k)n−k)=nk​(kn−k)\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{C_n}{k}=\frac{n}{n-(n-k)}\binom{n-(n-k)}{n-k}=\frac{n}{k}\binom{k}{n-k}

The summation limits are derived from the matching constraint 0≤m≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq m\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor. Substituting m=n−km=n-k leads to n−⌊n/2⌋≤k≤nn-\lfloor n/2\rfloor\leq k\leq n, which simplifies to ⌈n/2⌉≤k≤n\lceil n/2\rceil\leq k\leq n. Summing over these indices completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 3.8.

Let 𝒞⁡(G,1)=∑k[Gk]\mathcal{C}(G,1)=\sum_{k}{G\brack k} denote the total number of graphical cycle partitions of GG. The following relations hold:

  1. (1)

    For the cycle graph CnC_{n} (n≥3n\geq 3), the partition numbers are related to the Lucas numbers LnL_{n}:

    𝒞⁡(Cn,1)=Ln+1\mathcal{C}(C_{n},1)=L_{n}+1
  2. (2)

    For the path graph PnP_{n} (n≥1n\geq 1), the total number of partitions is given by the Fibonacci sequence:

    𝒞⁡(Pn,1)=Fn+1\mathcal{C}(P_{n},1)=F_{n+1}
Theorem 3.9.

For the complete graph KnK_{n}, the graphical cycle partition numbers [nk]{n\brack k} coincide with the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind [nk]{n\brack k}. Consequently, the graphical cycle polynomial of KnK_{n} is equivalent to the rising factorial:

𝒞⁡(Kn,x)=∑k=1n[nk]​xk=x⁡(x+1)​(x+2)​…​(x+n−1)\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}{n\brack k}x^{k}=x(x+1)(x+2)\dots(x+n-1)
Proof.

Recall that the Stirling number of the first kind counts the number of permutations of nn elements with kk disjoint cycles. In the complete graph KnK_{n}, any subset of mm vertices induces a clique where the number of possible oriented cycles is (m−1)!(m-1)! (with the convention that C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} yield 1).

Since every possible partition of the vertex set into kk subsets can be realized as a collection of kk cycles in KnK_{n}, the total count is:

[Knk]=∑{V1,…,Vk}∏i=1k(|Vi|−1)!{K_{n}\brack k}=\sum_{\{V_{1},\dots,V_{k}\}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}(|V_{i}|-1)!

This summation over all set partitions is the standard formula for the Stirling numbers of the first kind. ∎

The graphical cycle partition numbers [Gk]{G\brack k} provide a unified combinatorial framework that generalizes several classical sequences. The relationship between graph structure and these sequences is summarized in Table 3.

Theorem 3.10.

Let G+wvG+_{w}v denote the graph GG with an additional pendant vertex vv adjacent to w∈V⁡(G)w\in V(G). The graphical cycle polynomial of G+wvG+_{w}v is given by:

𝒞(G+wv,x)=x(𝒞(G,x)+𝒞(G−w,x))\mathcal{C}(G+_{w}v,x)=x\left(\mathcal{C}(G,x)+\mathcal{C}(G-w,x)\right)
Proof.

By Lemma 3.4, the coefficients of 𝒞(G+wv,x)\mathcal{C}(G+_{w}v,x) are [G+wvk]=[Gk−1]+[G−wk−1]{G+_{w}v\brack k}={G\brack k-1}+{G-w\brack k-1}. Substituting this into the generating function:

𝒞(G+wv,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(G+_{w}v,x) =∑k([Gk−1]+[G−wk−1])​xk\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\left({G\brack k-1}+{G-w\brack k-1}\right)x^{k}
=x​∑k[Gk−1]​xk−1+x​∑k[G−wk−1]​xk−1\displaystyle=x\sum_{k}{G\brack k-1}x^{k-1}+x\sum_{k}{G-w\brack k-1}x^{k-1}
=x​𝒞​(G,x)+x​𝒞​(G−w,x)\displaystyle=x\mathcal{C}(G,x)+x\mathcal{C}(G-w,x)

as required. ∎

The following results establish the fundamental recurrence relations for the graphical Stirling numbers of the first kind [Gk]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}. These results facilitate the recursive computation of the graphical cycle polynomial for graphs with specific local structures.

Theorem 3.11 (Reduction Theorem).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a simple graph and v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G). If vv is not contained in any induced cycle of length ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3 in GG, then the graphical Stirling numbers of the first kind satisfy the recurrence:

[Gk]=[G−vk−1]+∑w∈N⁡(v)[G−{v,w}k−1]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{w\in N(v)}\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}

In the case where the neighborhood N⁡(v)N(v) is vertex-transitive within GG (i.e., G−{v,wi}≅G−{v,wj}G-\{v,w_{i}\}\cong G-\{v,w_{j}\} for all wi,wj∈N⁡(v)w_{i},w_{j}\in N(v)), the recurrence simplifies to:

[Gk]=[G−vk−1]+deg⁡(v)​[G−{v,w}k−1]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}+\deg(v)\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}

for any arbitrary neighbor w∈N⁡(v)w\in N(v).

Proof.

Let v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) be a vertex that is not contained in any induced cycle of length ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3. We partition the set of all kk-cycle partitions of GG based on the block BB containing vv. By the given condition, BB must induce a Hamiltonian cycle, but since vv belongs to no induced cycles of length ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3, the only possibilities are |B|=1|B|=1 or |B|=2|B|=2.

  • •

    Case 1 (|B|=1|B|=1): If B={v}B=\{v\}, the remaining vertices must be partitioned into k−1k-1 cycles in G−vG-v, giving [G−vk−1]\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix} ways.

  • •

    Case 2 (|B|=2|B|=2): If B={v,w}B=\{v,w\} for w∈N⁡(v)w\in N(v), the remaining vertices must be partitioned into k−1k-1 cycles in G−{v,w}G-\{v,w\}. Summing over all w∈N⁡(v)w\in N(v) gives ∑w∈N⁡(v)[G−{v,w}k−1]\sum_{w\in N(v)}\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}.

If N⁡(v)N(v) is vertex-transitive, then for all wi,wj∈N⁡(v)w_{i},w_{j}\in N(v), the subgraphs G−{v,wi}G-\{v,w_{i}\} and G−{v,wj}G-\{v,w_{j}\} are isomorphic, implying [G−{v,wi}k−1]=[G−{v,wj}k−1]\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w_{i}\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w_{j}\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}. Summing over the deg⁡(v)\deg(v) neighbors yields the simplified form. ∎

Example 3.12.

When G=KnG=K_{n}, the graphical Stirling numbers [Knk]\begin{bmatrix}K_{n}\\ k\end{bmatrix} correspond exactly to the classical Stirling numbers of the first kind [nk]\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}.

Applying the theorem 3.11 to KnK_{n} with vertex vv:

  1. (1)

    The subgraph G−vG-v is isomorphic to Kn−1K_{n-1}.

  2. (2)

    The degree of any vertex in KnK_{n} is deg⁡(v)=n−1\deg(v)=n-1.

  3. (3)

    In a complete graph, the contribution of the neighbors is uniform. The recurrence simplifies to the classical identity:

[nk]=[n−1k−1]+(n−1)​[n−1k]\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}n-1\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}+(n-1)\begin{bmatrix}n-1\\ k\end{bmatrix}

This example confirms that the graphical recurrence is a structural generalization of the classical combinatorial identity, where the ”multiplier” (n−1)(n-1) is replaced by the specific adjacency constraints (the degree) of the vertex in a general graph GG.

Corollary 3.13.

If vv is a leaf (pendant vertex) with neighbor ww, then:

[Gk]=[G−vk−1]+[G−{v,w}k−1]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}

This confirms that for paths and trees, the graphical Stirling distribution is inherently linked to the matching polynomial of the graph.

Remark 3.14.

The ”No ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3 cycle” condition is necessary for the simplicity of the theorem. Consider the Wheel graph WnW_{n} with central hub hh. If we apply the reduction to hh, the summation over N⁡(h)N(h) is insufficient because hh is contained in many 3-cycles of the form {h,vi,vi+1}\{h,v_{i},v_{i+1}\}. In such cases, the recurrence must be extended to include a summation over all CℓC_{\ell} subgraphs containing vv:

[Gk]=[G−vk−1]+∑w∈N⁡(v)[G−{v,w}k−1]+∑C∈𝒞⁡(v),|C|≥3[G−V⁡(C)k−1]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{w\in N(v)}\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}(v),|C|\geq 3}\begin{bmatrix}G-V(C)\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}

where 𝒞⁡(v)\mathcal{C}(v) is the set of all cycles in GG passing through vv.

Corollary 3.15.

Let S1,n−1S_{1,n-1} be the star graph on nn vertices. Then the graphical cycle polynomial of the first kind of S1,n−1S_{1,n-1} is

𝒞⁡(S1,n−1,x)=xn+(n−1)​xn−1.\mathcal{C}(S_{1,n-1},x)=x^{n}+(n-1)x^{n-1}.
Proof.

Let vv be the central vertex of S1,n−1S_{1,n-1} and let u1,…,un−1u_{1},\dots,u_{n-1} be its leaves. Since S1,n−1S_{1,n-1} is a tree, it contains no cycles. Consequently, no induced subgraph on more than two vertices is Hamiltonian. By the definition of graphical cycle partitions, every block in a graphical cycle partition of S1,n−1S_{1,n-1} therefore has size at most 22.

The only blocks of size 22 that may occur are edges of the graph. As the only edges of S1,n−1S_{1,n-1} are {v,ui}\{v,u_{i}\} for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, any graphical cycle partition contains at most one 22-cycle, since all such edges share the vertex vv.

If no 22-cycle is chosen, then every vertex appears as a 11-cycle, yielding a unique graphical cycle partition with nn blocks. If a 22-cycle {v,ui}\{v,u_{i}\} is chosen, then the remaining n−2n-2 vertices must appear as 11-cycles, yielding a graphical cycle partition with n−1n-1 blocks. There are n−1n-1 such partitions, corresponding to the choice of the leaf uiu_{i}.

No other graphical cycle partitions are possible. Therefore,

𝒞⁡(S1,n−1,x)=xn+(n−1)​xn−1,\mathcal{C}(S_{1,n-1},x)=x^{n}+(n-1)x^{n-1},

as claimed. ∎

Theorem 3.16.

For a tree TnT_{n}, if vv is a leaf vertex with unique neighbor uu, then:

𝒞⁡(Tn,x)=x​𝒞​(Tn−v,x)+x​𝒞​(Tn−{v,u},x)\mathcal{C}(T_{n},x)=x\mathcal{C}(T_{n}-v,x)+x\mathcal{C}(T_{n}-\{v,u\},x)
Proof.

In any tree TnT_{n}, there are no induced cycles of length ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3. Thus, Theorem 3.11 applies to any vertex. By choosing vv to be a leaf, the set N⁡(v)N(v) contains only the vertex uu. The summation reduces to a single term. ∎

Theorem 3.17.

Let F=⋃i=1mTiF=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}T_{i} be a forest. Then 𝒞⁡(F,x)=∏i=1m𝒞⁡(Ti,x)\mathcal{C}(F,x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{C}(T_{i},x).

Proof.

The proof follows immediately from the combination of Theorems 3.11 and 3.3. ∎

Theorem 3.18.

Let GG be a simple graph and v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G). If vv is not contained in any induced cycle of length ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3, the graphical cycle polynomial satisfies:

𝒞⁡(G,x)=x⁡(𝒞⁡(G−v,x)+∑w∈N⁡(v)𝒞⁡(G−{v,w},x))\mathcal{C}(G,x)=x\left(\mathcal{C}(G-v,x)+\sum_{w\in N(v)}\mathcal{C}(G-\{v,w\},x)\right)
Proof.

By Theorem 3.11, the coefficients of 𝒞⁡(G,x)\mathcal{C}(G,x) are given by:

[Gk]=[G−vk−1]+∑w∈N⁡(v)[G−{v,w}k−1]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{w\in N(v)}\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}

Multiplying both sides by xkx^{k} and summing over all possible values of kk:

∑k[Gk]​xk\displaystyle\sum_{k}\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}x^{k} =∑k[G−vk−1]​xk+∑k(∑w∈N⁡(v)[G−{v,w}k−1])​xk\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}x^{k}+\sum_{k}\left(\sum_{w\in N(v)}\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}\right)x^{k}
=x​∑k[G−vk−1]​xk−1+x​∑w∈N⁡(v)(∑k[G−{v,w}k−1]​xk−1)\displaystyle=x\sum_{k}\begin{bmatrix}G-v\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}x^{k-1}+x\sum_{w\in N(v)}\left(\sum_{k}\begin{bmatrix}G-\{v,w\}\\ k-1\end{bmatrix}x^{k-1}\right)

Recognizing the definitions of the polynomials for the subgraphs, we obtain:

𝒞⁡(G,x)=x​𝒞​(G−v,x)+x​∑w∈N⁡(v)𝒞⁡(G−{v,w},x)\mathcal{C}(G,x)=x\mathcal{C}(G-v,x)+x\sum_{w\in N(v)}\mathcal{C}(G-\{v,w\},x)

This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma 3.19 (Broom Lemma).

Let BB be a set of ℓ\ell isolated vertices. Let G+wBG+_{w}B denote the graph obtained by attaching each vertex in BB to w∈V⁡(G)w\in V(G) via a pendant edge. The graphical cycle partition numbers satisfy:

[G+wBk]=[Gk−ℓ]+ℓ​[G−wk−ℓ]\begin{bmatrix}G+_{w}B\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k-\ell\end{bmatrix}+\ell\begin{bmatrix}G-w\\ k-\ell\end{bmatrix}
Proof.

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a kk-cycle partition of G+wBG+_{w}B. Each v∈Bv\in B is a pendant vertex and thus can only be part of a C1C_{1} or a C2C_{2} induced by the edge incident to ww. Since all edges incident to BB share the vertex ww, the partition can contain at most one C2C_{2} from the set of edges {w​vi∣vi∈B}\{wv_{i}\mid v_{i}\in B\}.

  • •

    If no C2C_{2} is formed using vertices from BB, then all ℓ\ell vertices in BB form individual 11-cycles. The remaining k−ℓk-\ell cycles must partition GG, giving [Gk−ℓ]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k-\ell\end{bmatrix} ways.

  • •

    If exactly one vertex vi∈Bv_{i}\in B forms a C2C_{2} with ww, there are ℓ\ell choices for viv_{i}. The remaining ℓ−1\ell-1 vertices in BB must form 11-cycles. This accounts for ℓ\ell cycles in total. The remaining k−ℓk-\ell cycles must partition G−wG-w, giving ℓ​[G−wk−ℓ]\ell\begin{bmatrix}G-w\\ k-\ell\end{bmatrix} ways.

The sum of these two disjoint cases yields the identity. ∎

Theorem 3.20 (Broom Polynomial Identity).

The graphical cycle polynomial for the brooming operation is:

𝒞(G+wB,x)=xℓ(𝒞(G,x)+ℓ𝒞(G−w,x))\mathcal{C}(G+_{w}B,x)=x^{\ell}\left(\mathcal{C}(G,x)+\ell\mathcal{C}(G-w,x)\right)
Theorem 3.21.

Let G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} be disjoint graphs.

  1. (1)

    Let Gb​r​i​d​g​eG_{bridge} be formed by connecting u∈V⁡(G1)u\in V(G_{1}) and v∈V⁡(G2)v\in V(G_{2}) via a bridge e={u,v}e=\{u,v\}. The graphical Stirling numbers and the cycle polynomial satisfy:

    [Gb​r​i​d​g​ek]=∑i[G1i]​[G2k−i]+∑j[G1−uj]​[G2−vk−1−j]\begin{bmatrix}G_{bridge}\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{i}\begin{bmatrix}G_{1}\\ i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}G_{2}\\ k-i\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{j}\begin{bmatrix}G_{1}-u\\ j\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}G_{2}-v\\ k-1-j\end{bmatrix}
    𝒞⁡(Gb​r​i​d​g​e,x)=𝒞⁡(G1,x)​𝒞​(G2,x)+x​𝒞​(G1−u,x)​𝒞​(G2−v,x)\mathcal{C}(G_{bridge},x)=\mathcal{C}(G_{1},x)\mathcal{C}(G_{2},x)+x\mathcal{C}(G_{1}-u,x)\mathcal{C}(G_{2}-v,x)
  2. (2)

    Let Gc​o​a​l=G1⋅wG2G_{coal}=G_{1}\cdot_{w}G_{2} be the graph formed by identifying u∈V⁡(G1)u\in V(G_{1}) and v∈V⁡(G2)v\in V(G_{2}) into a shared vertex ww. The graphical Stirling numbers and the cycle polynomial satisfy:

    [Gc​o​a​lk]=∑i+j=k+1[G1i]​[G2j],𝒞⁡(Gc​o​a​l,x)=1x​𝒞​(G1,x)​𝒞​(G2,x)\begin{bmatrix}G_{coal}\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{i+j=k+1}\begin{bmatrix}G_{1}\\ i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}G_{2}\\ j\end{bmatrix},\quad\mathcal{C}(G_{coal},x)=\frac{1}{x}\mathcal{C}(G_{1},x)\mathcal{C}(G_{2},x)
Proof.

For the bridge join, we partition the cycle configurations based on the bridge ee. If ee is not a block, uu and vv belong to separate sub-partitions of G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, leading to the first summation. If ee is a block, it is a K2K_{2} cycle, and we partition the remaining V⁡(G1−u)∪V⁡(G2−v)V(G_{1}-u)\cup V(G_{2}-v) vertices into k−1k-1 blocks, yielding the second summation.

For (2), ww is a cut-vertex. Any induced cycle containing ww lies strictly in G1G_{1} or G2G_{2}. The identification of ww merges the two independent partitions into a single configuration with k=i+j−1k=i+j-1 blocks. Summing over all valid indices gives the result. ∎

Example 3.22 (Barbell Graph BnB_{n}).

The Barbell graph BnB_{n} is obtained by connecting two disjoint complete graphs KnK_{n} via a bridge e={u,v}e=\{u,v\}, where uu and vv are vertices in the respective cliques. By the Bridge Lemma (Lemma 3.21), the graphical Stirling numbers of the first kind are given by

[Bnk]=∑i[ni]​[nk−i]+∑j[n−1j]​[n−1k−1−j].\begin{bmatrix}B_{n}\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{i}\begin{bmatrix}n\\ i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k-i\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{j}\begin{bmatrix}n-1\\ j\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}n-1\\ k-1-j\end{bmatrix}.

This decomposition shows that the cycle partitions of a Barbell graph are governed by the convolution of classical Stirling numbers for the full cliques and for the reduced cliques of order n−1n-1.

Corollary 3.23.

The cycle polynomial of the Barbell graph satisfies the recurrence

𝒞⁡(Bn,x)=𝒞​(Kn,x)2+x​𝒞​(Kn−1,x)2,\mathcal{C}(B_{n},x)=\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)^{2}+x\,\mathcal{C}(K_{n-1},x)^{2},

and it is real-rooted.

Proof.

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the set of all cycle partitions of BnB_{n}. Partition 𝒫\mathcal{P} according to the status of the bridge e={u,v}e=\{u,v\}:

  • •

    Case 1: ee is not a block. The vertices uu and vv belong to separate blocks within their respective cliques. The number of such partitions is the product of the partitions of the two independent KnK_{n} graphs:

    𝒞⁡(Kn,x)⋅𝒞⁡(Kn,x)=𝒞​(Kn,x)2.\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)\cdot\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)=\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)^{2}.
  • •

    Case 2: ee forms a block. The bridge forms an independent K2K_{2} block. The remaining n−1n-1 vertices in each clique are partitioned independently, contributing

    x⋅𝒞⁡(Kn−1,x)⋅𝒞⁡(Kn−1,x)=x​𝒞​(Kn−1,x)2,x\cdot\mathcal{C}(K_{n-1},x)\cdot\mathcal{C}(K_{n-1},x)=x\,\mathcal{C}(K_{n-1},x)^{2},

    where the factor xx accounts for the new block.

Combining the two cases gives the structural recurrence:

𝒞⁡(Bn,x)=𝒞​(Kn,x)2+x​𝒞​(Kn−1,x)2.\mathcal{C}(B_{n},x)=\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)^{2}+x\,\mathcal{C}(K_{n-1},x)^{2}.

Recall that 𝒞⁡(Kn,x)=xn¯\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)=x^{\overline{n}}, the rising factorial. Using xn¯=(x+n−1)​xn−1¯x^{\overline{n}}=(x+n-1)x^{\overline{n-1}}, we factor (xn−1¯)2(x^{\overline{n-1}})^{2}:

𝒞⁡(Bn,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(B_{n},x) =((x+n−1)​xn−1¯)2+x​(xn−1¯)2\displaystyle=\bigl((x+n-1)x^{\overline{n-1}}\bigr)^{2}+x\,(x^{\overline{n-1}})^{2}
=(xn−1¯)2​((x+n−1)2+x)\displaystyle=(x^{\overline{n-1}})^{2}\bigl((x+n-1)^{2}+x\bigr)
=(xn−1¯)2​[x2+(2​n−1)​x+(n−1)2].\displaystyle=(x^{\overline{n-1}})^{2}\left[x^{2}+(2n-1)x+(n-1)^{2}\right].

The quadratic factor has discriminant

Δ=(2​n−1)2−4​(n−1)2=4​n−3>0,\Delta=(2n-1)^{2}-4(n-1)^{2}=4n-3>0,

which ensures that all roots are real. Since xn−1¯x^{\overline{n-1}} is also real-rooted, it follows that 𝒞⁡(Bn,x)\mathcal{C}(B_{n},x) is real-rooted. ∎

Example 3.24 (Tadpole Graph Tn,mT_{n,m}).

The Tadpole graph Tn,mT_{n,m} is the union of a cycle CnC_{n} and a path PmP_{m} connected by a bridge. By applying the Lemma 3.21, the graphical cycle stirling numbers is given by:

[Tn,mk]=∑i[Cni]​[Pmk−i]+∑j[Cn−1j]​[Pm−1k−1−j].\begin{bmatrix}T_{n,m}\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{i}\begin{bmatrix}C_{n}\\ i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P_{m}\\ k-i\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{j}\begin{bmatrix}C_{n-1}\\ j\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P_{m-1}\\ k-1-j\end{bmatrix}.

Substituting the established binomial closed-form expressions for path and cycle graphical Stirling numbers:

[Tn,mk]=∑i(im−i)⁡[(k−i−1n−k+i)+2​(k−i−1n−k+i−1)]+∑j(jm−1−j)​(k−j−1n−k+j).\begin{bmatrix}T_{n,m}\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{i}\binom{i}{m-i}\left[\binom{k-i-1}{n-k+i}+2\binom{k-i-1}{n-k+i-1}\right]+\sum_{j}\binom{j}{m-1-j}\binom{k-j-1}{n-k+j}.

The first summation accounts for partitions where the bridge is not a block, while the second summation accounts for partitions where the bridge {u,v}\{u,v\} forms an edge-block, effectively reducing the components to Pm−1P_{m-1} and Pn−1P_{n-1}.

Corollary 3.25 (Closed Form for Tadpole Graph Tn,mT_{n,m}).

The cycle polynomial of the Tadpole graph Tn,mT_{n,m} can be expressed in terms of Lucas polynomials ln​(x)l_{n}(x) and Fibonacci polynomials fn​(x)f_{n}(x) as:

𝒞⁡(Tn,m,x)=ln​(x)​fm​(x)+x​fn−1​(x)​fm−1​(x)\mathcal{C}(T_{n,m},x)=l_{n}(x)f_{m}(x)+xf_{n-1}(x)f_{m-1}(x)

and it is real-rooted.

Proof.

Let e={u,v}e=\{u,v\} be the bridge connecting CnC_{n} and PmP_{m}. By the Bridge Lemma, we partition the cycle partitions 𝒫⁡(Tn,m)\mathcal{P}(T_{n,m}) into two disjoint sets: those where ee is not an edge-block and those where ee is an edge-block.

  1. (1)

    Case 1: e∉Blocks​(π)e\notin\text{Blocks}(\pi). The generating function is the product of the component polynomials: 𝒞⁡(Cn,x)​𝒞​(Pm,x)\mathcal{C}(C_{n},x)\mathcal{C}(P_{m},x).

  2. (2)

    Case 2: e∈Blocks​(π)e\in\text{Blocks}(\pi). This contributes x1x^{1} and reduces the remaining graph to Pn−1∪Pm−1P_{n-1}\cup P_{m-1}. The generating function is x​𝒞​(Pn−1,x)​𝒞​(Pm−1,x)x\mathcal{C}(P_{n-1},x)\mathcal{C}(P_{m-1},x).

Since CnC_{n} and PnP_{n} have Lucas and Fibonacci polynomials as their respective cycle polynomials, the closed form follows. The convolution for the coefficients [Tn,mk]\begin{bmatrix}T_{n,m}\\ k\end{bmatrix} is obtained by applying the Cauchy product rule to the polynomial multiplication and accounting for the index shift in the second term. ∎

Example 3.26 (Lollipop Graph Ln,mL_{n,m}).

The Lollipop graph Ln,mL_{n,m} is formed by joining a complete graph KnK_{n} to a path PmP_{m} via a bridge connecting a vertex of KnK_{n} to an endpoint of PmP_{m}. By the Bridge Lemma (Lemma 3.21), the graphical rr-Stirling numbers of the first kind satisfy

[Ln,mk]=∑i[ni]​[Pmk−i]+∑j[n−1j]​[Pm−1k−1−j].\begin{bmatrix}L_{n,m}\\ k\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{i}\begin{bmatrix}n\\ i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P_{m}\\ k-i\end{bmatrix}+\sum_{j}\begin{bmatrix}n-1\\ j\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P_{m-1}\\ k-1-j\end{bmatrix}.

This decomposition separates partitions according to whether the bridge forms an independent block.

Theorem 3.27 (Closed Form and Rootedness of Lollipop Graphs).

The cycle polynomial of the Lollipop graph Ln,mL_{n,m} is given by:

𝒞⁡(Ln,m,x)=xn−1¯​[(x+n−1)​fm​(x)+x​fm−1​(x)]\mathcal{C}(L_{n,m},x)=x^{\overline{n-1}}\left[(x+n-1)f_{m}(x)+xf_{m-1}(x)\right]

where fm​(x)f_{m}(x) is the Fibonacci polynomial of order mm. The sequence of graphical Stirling numbers [Ln,mk]\begin{bmatrix}L_{n,m}\\ k\end{bmatrix} is real-rooted.

Proof.

By applying the Bridge Lemma to the edge ee connecting KnK_{n} and PmP_{m}, we obtain:

𝒞⁡(Ln,m,x)=𝒞⁡(Kn,x)​fm​(x)+x​𝒞​(Kn−1,x)​fm−1​(x).\mathcal{C}(L_{n,m},x)=\mathcal{C}(K_{n},x)f_{m}(x)+x\mathcal{C}(K_{n-1},x)f_{m-1}(x).

Substituting xn¯=(x+n−1)​xn−1¯x^{\overline{n}}=(x+n-1)x^{\overline{n-1}} allows for the factorization of xn−1¯x^{\overline{n-1}}. Real-rootedness is guaranteed by the interlacing properties of Fibonacci polynomials and the fact that xn−1¯x^{\overline{n-1}} consists of n−1n-1 distinct linear factors with real roots. ∎

4. Graphical rr-Stirling Numbers of the First Kind

Definition 4.1 (Graphical rr-Stirling Number).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a simple graph of order nn. For 1≤r≤k≤n1\leq r\leq k\leq n, the graphical rr-Stirling number of the first kind, denoted by [Gk]r{G\brack k}_{r}, is defined as the number of partitions of V⁡(G)V(G) into kk blocks {C1,C2,…,Ck}\{C_{1},C_{2},\dots,C_{k}\} such that:

  1. (1)

    Each induced subgraph G⁡[Ci]G[C_{i}] is a 11-cycle, a 22-cycle, or a Hamiltonian subgraph of order |Ci|≥3|C_{i}|\geq 3.

  2. (2)

    The first rr labeled vertices {1,2,…,r}\{1,2,\dots,r\} are contained in distinct blocks.

Definition 4.2 (Graphical rr-Cycle Polynomial).

Let GG be a simple graph of order nn. For a non-negative integer rr such that 0≤r≤n0\leq r\leq n, we define the graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind, denoted by 𝒞r​(G,x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(G,x), as the generating function:

𝒞r​(G,x)=∑k=rn[Gk]r​xk,\mathcal{C}_{r}(G,x)=\sum_{k=r}^{n}{G\brack k}_{r}x^{k},

where [Gk]r{G\brack k}_{r} denotes the graphical rr-Stirling number of the first kind. In the case where r=1r=1 (or r=0r=0), we simply write 𝒞⁡(G,x)\mathcal{C}(G,x).

Theorem 4.3.

Let nn be a positive integer and R⊆V⁡(Kn)R\subseteq V(K_{n}) be a set of rr restricted vertices where 1≤r≤n1\leq r\leq n. The following properties hold for the complete graph KnK_{n}:

  1. (i)

    Classical Correspondence: The rr-restricted graphical Stirling numbers of the first kind coincide exactly with the classical rr-Stirling numbers:

    [Knk]r=[nk]r.\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{K_n}{k}\right]_{r}=\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{r}.
  2. (ii)

    Generating Function: The rr-restricted graphical cycle polynomial of KnK_{n} is given by the restricted rising factorial:

    𝒞r​(Kn,x)=∑k=rn[nk]r​xk=xr​∏i=rn−1(x+i).\mathcal{C}_{r}(K_{n},x)=\sum_{k=r}^{n}\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{r}x^{k}=x^{r}\prod_{i=r}^{n-1}(x+i).
  3. (iii)

    Recurrence Relation: For n>rn>r, the graphical Stirling numbers satisfy:

    [Knk]r=[Kn−1k−1]r+(n−1)​[Kn−1k]r.\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{K_n}{k}\right]_{r}=\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{K_{n-1}}{k-1}\right]_{r}+(n-1)\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{K_{n-1}}{k}\right]_{r}.
Proof.

We proceed by induction on nn for parts (i) and (iii). Base case: For n=rn=r, the rr-restriction requires each vertex in RR to belong to a distinct cycle. Since there are only rr vertices total, each must form a 1-cycle. Thus, [Krr]r=1\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{K_r}{r}\right]_{r}=1, which matches the classical boundary condition [rr]r=1\begin{bmatrix}r\\ r\end{bmatrix}_{r}=1.

Inductive step: Assume the result holds for n−1n-1. Consider KnK_{n} and an unrestricted vertex v∈V⁡(Kn)∖Rv\in V(K_{n})\setminus R. In any rr-restricted cycle partition into kk cycles, vertex vv has two options:

  1. (1)

    vv forms its own 1-cycle (C1C_{1}). The remaining n−1n-1 vertices are partitioned into k−1k-1 cycles satisfying rr restrictions. This gives [Kn−1k−1]r\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{K_{n-1}}{k-1}\right]_{r} ways.

  2. (2)

    vv is part of a cycle of length ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2. In KnK_{n}, vv can be inserted into any of the n−1n-1 existing edge-slots of a valid cycle partition of Kn−1K_{n-1} to form a larger cycle. This gives (n−1)​[Kn−1k]r(n-1)\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{K_{n-1}}{k}\right]_{r} ways.

Summing these cases yields the recurrence in (iii). Since this recurrence and the boundary conditions are identical to the classical rr-Stirling numbers, the identity in (i) is proven. Part (ii) follows immediately as the generating function for said coefficients. ∎

Corollary 4.4.

The total number of rr-restricted cycle partitions of KnK_{n}, denoted Br​(Kn)B_{r}(K_{n}), is given by:

Br​(Kn)=n!r!.B_{r}(K_{n})=\frac{n!}{r!}.
Proof.

The total number of partitions is found by evaluating the cycle polynomial at x=1x=1:

Br(Kn)=𝒞r(Kn,1)=1r∏i=rn−1(1+i)=(r+1)(r+2)⋯(n)=n!r!.B_{r}(K_{n})=\mathcal{C}_{r}(K_{n},1)=1^{r}\prod_{i=r}^{n-1}(1+i)=(r+1)(r+2)\cdots(n)=\frac{n!}{r!}.

∎

Theorem 4.5.

Let n,k∈ℕn,k\in\mathbb{N} and let PnP_{n} be a path graph with nn vertices. For 1≤r≤k≤n1\leq r\leq k\leq n, the graphical rr-Stirling number of the first kind is given by:

[Pnk]r=(k−r+1n−k).{P_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}.

Furthermore, the total number of such graphical rr-cycle partitions is given by:

Br​(Pn)=∑k=rn[Pnk]r=Fn−r+1,B_{r}(P_{n})=\sum_{k=r}^{n}{P_{n}\brack k}_{r}=F_{n-r+1},

where FmF_{m} denotes the mm-th Fibonacci number.

Proof.

Let the vertices of PnP_{n} be sequentially labeled {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\}. Since PnP_{n} contains no cycles of length greater than 2, any graphical cycle partition must consist only of 11-cycles (singleton vertices) and 22-cycles (edges).

The rr-restriction requires that the vertices {1,2,…,r}\{1,2,\dots,r\} belong to distinct blocks. Note that for any i<ri<r, the vertex ii cannot be part of a 22-cycle with i+1i+1, as i+1i+1 must also occupy its own distinct block. Consequently, the vertices {1,2,…,r−1}\{1,2,\dots,r-1\} are forced to form r−1r-1 distinct 11-cycles.

We now consider the placement of vertex rr. There are two exhaustive cases for the block CC containing rr:

  • •

    Case I: C={r}C=\{r\} is a 11-cycle. We must then partition the remaining n−rn-r vertices into k−rk-r blocks. The number of ways to partition NN vertices into KK blocks of size 1 or 2 is (KN−K)\binom{K}{N-K}. Thus, there are (k−rn−r−(k−r))=(k−rn−k)\binom{k-r}{n-r-(k-r)}=\binom{k-r}{n-k} such partitions.

  • •

    Case II: C={r,r+1}C=\{r,r+1\} is a 22-cycle. We must then partition the remaining n−(r+1)n-(r+1) vertices into k−rk-r remaining blocks. This results in (k−rn−r−1−(k−r))=(k−rn−k−1)\binom{k-r}{n-r-1-(k-r)}=\binom{k-r}{n-k-1} partitions.

Summing these cases and applying Pascal’s identity, we obtain:

[Pnk]r=(k−rn−k)+(k−rn−k−1)=(k−r+1n−k).{P_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\binom{k-r}{n-k}+\binom{k-r}{n-k-1}=\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}.

To compute the total number of partitions, we sum over all possible values of kk:

∑k=rn[Pnk]r=∑k=rn(k−r+1n−k).\sum_{k=r}^{n}{P_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\sum_{k=r}^{n}\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}.

By performing the change of variable j=k−rj=k-r, the sum becomes ∑j=0n−r(j+1n−r−j)\sum_{j=0}^{n-r}\binom{j+1}{n-r-j}. Using the well-known identity for the sum along the shallow diagonals of Pascal’s triangle, ∑i=0⌊m/2⌋(m−ii)=Fm+1\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\binom{m-i}{i}=F_{m+1}, we find:

Br​(Pn)=∑k=rn[Pnk]r=Fn−r+1.B_{r}(P_{n})=\sum_{k=r}^{n}{P_{n}\brack k}_{r}=F_{n-r+1}.

This completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 4.6.

The rr-restricted graphical cycle polynomial for the path graph PnP_{n} is defined by:

Cr​(Pn,x)=xr−1​C​(Pn−r+1,x).C_{r}(P_{n},x)=x^{r-1}C(P_{n-r+1},x).

By expanding the sum, the polynomial can be expressed as:

Cr​(Pn,x)=∑j=0⌊n−r+12⌋(n−r+1−jj)​xn−j.C_{r}(P_{n},x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n-r+1}{2}\rfloor}\binom{n-r+1-j}{j}x^{n-j}.

Furthermore, for n≥r+2n\geq r+2, the polynomial satisfies the following recurrence relation:

Cr​(Pn,x)=x​Cr​(Pn−1,x)+x​Cr​(Pn−2,x),C_{r}(P_{n},x)=xC_{r}(P_{n-1},x)+xC_{r}(P_{n-2},x),

with the initial conditions Cr​(Pr,x)=xrC_{r}(P_{r},x)=x^{r} and Cr​(Pr+1,x)=xr+1+xrC_{r}(P_{r+1},x)=x^{r+1}+x^{r}.

Proof.

Substituting the result [Pnk]r=(k−r+1n−k){P_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\binom{k-r+1}{n-k} into the definition of the graphical rr-cycle polynomial yields:

𝒞r​(Pn,x)=∑k=rn[Pnk]r​xk=∑k=rn(k−r+1n−k)​xk.\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n},x)=\sum_{k=r}^{n}{P_{n}\brack k}_{r}x^{k}=\sum_{k=r}^{n}\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}x^{k}.

Applying the change of variable j=k−rj=k-r, such that k=j+rk=j+r, we shift the summation index:

𝒞r​(Pn,x)=∑j=0n−r(j+1n−r−j)​xj+r=xr​∑j=0n−r(j+1n−r−j)​xj.\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n},x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-r}\binom{j+1}{n-r-j}x^{j+r}=x^{r}\sum_{j=0}^{n-r}\binom{j+1}{n-r-j}x^{j}.

To verify the recurrence for n≥r+2n\geq r+2, we consider the terminal vertex vnv_{n}. In any rr-graphical partition, vnv_{n} belongs to a block CC. Since PnP_{n} is a path, CC is either a 11-cycle {vn}\{v_{n}\} or a 22-cycle {vn−1,vn}\{v_{n-1},v_{n}\}.

  • •

    If C={vn}C=\{v_{n}\}, the remaining vertices form a valid rr-graphical partition of Pn−1P_{n-1}. This contributes x​𝒞r​(Pn−1,x)x\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n-1},x).

  • •

    If C={vn−1,vn}C=\{v_{n-1},v_{n}\}, the remaining vertices form a valid rr-graphical partition of Pn−2P_{n-2}. Since n−1>rn-1>r, the rr-restriction is not violated. This contributes x​𝒞r​(Pn−2,x)x\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n-2},x).

The summation of these cases confirms the recurrence. The base cases follow directly: for PrP_{r}, only rr singletons are allowed (xrx^{r}); for Pr+1P_{r+1}, we may have r+1r+1 singletons (xr+1x^{r+1}) or the edge {r,r+1}\{r,r+1\} with r−1r-1 singletons (xrx^{r}). ∎

The complement of the path graph, PncP_{n}^{c}, represents a ”nearly-complete” structure. Its cycle-forming properties are governed by a shifted recurrence that reflects the removal of specific edges from the complete graph KnK_{n}.

Theorem 4.7.

Let PncP_{n}^{c} denote the complement of the path graph PnP_{n} on nn vertices.

    Case 2: vnv_{n} is inserted into an existing cycle. In the cycle notation of a permutation, a vertex vnv_{n} can be inserted immediately following any vertex uu provided the edge (u,vn)(u,v_{n}) exists in the graph. Since vnv_{n} is adjacent to n−2n-2 vertices in PncP_{n}^{c}, there are exactly n−2n-2 such insertion sites. This contributes (n−2)​[Pn−1ck]r(n-2)\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{P_{n-1}^c}{k}\right]_{r} ways.

Summing these cases yields the recurrence in (ii), and setting r=1r=1 yields (i).

Using the definition of the cycle polynomial 𝒞r​(Pnc,x)=∑k=rn[Pnck]r​xk\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n}^{c},x)=\sum_{k=r}^{n}\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{P_n^c}{k}\right]_{r}x^{k} and substituting the recurrence from (ii):

𝒞r​(Pnc,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n}^{c},x) =∑k([Pn−1ck−1]r+(n−2)​[Pn−1ck]r)​xk\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\left(\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{P_{n-1}^c}{k-1}\right]_{r}+(n-2)\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{P_{n-1}^c}{k}\right]_{r}\right)x^{k}
=∑k[Pn−1ck−1]r​xk+(n−2)​∑k[Pn−1ck]r​xk\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{P_{n-1}^c}{k-1}\right]_{r}x^{k}+(n-2)\sum_{k}\left[\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{P_{n-1}^c}{k}\right]_{r}x^{k}
=x​𝒞r​(Pn−1c,x)+(n−2)​𝒞r​(Pn−1c,x)\displaystyle=x\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n-1}^{c},x)+(n-2)\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n-1}^{c},x)
=(x+n−2)​𝒞r​(Pn−1c,x).\displaystyle=(x+n-2)\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n-1}^{c},x).

This completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 4.8.

The graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind for PncP_{n}^{c} is given by:

𝒞r​(Pnc,x)=xr​∏i=r−1n−3(x+i).\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n}^{c},x)=x^{r}\prod_{i=r-1}^{n-3}(x+i).

We proceed by induction on nn for a fixed restriction parameter rr. Let n=rn=r. For a graph where all vertices are restricted, each vertex must occupy a distinct 1-cycle. Thus, 𝒞r​(Prc,x)=xr\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{r}^{c},x)=x^{r}. Applying the formula:

xr​∏i=r−1r−2(x+i)=xr⋅(1)=xr.x^{r}\prod_{i=r-1}^{r-2}(x+i)=x^{r}\cdot(1)=x^{r}.

The base case holds for the empty product.

𝒞r​(Pn−1c,x)=xr​∏i=r−1n−3(x+i).\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n-1}^{c},x)=x^{r}\prod_{i=r-1}^{n-3}(x+i).

=xr​[∏i=r−1n−3(x+i)]⋅(x+n−2).\displaystyle=x^{r}\left[\prod_{i=r-1}^{n-3}(x+i)\right]\cdot(x+n-2).

By extending the product to the upper limit n−2n-2, we obtain:

𝒞r​(Pnc,x)=xr​∏i=r−1n−2(x+i).\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n}^{c},x)=x^{r}\prod_{i=r-1}^{n-2}(x+i).

Remark 4.9.

It is instructive to compare this result with the polynomial for the complete graph KnK_{n}:

  • •

    𝒞r​(Kn,x)=xr​(x+r)​(x+r+1)​…​(x+n−1)\mathcal{C}_{r}(K_{n},x)=x^{r}(x+r)(x+r+1)\dots(x+n-1)

    𝒞r​(Pnc,x)=xr​(x+r−1)​(x+r)​…​(x+n−2)\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n}^{c},x)=x^{r}(x+r-1)(x+r)\dots(x+n-2)

The removal of the path edges PnP_{n} from KnK_{n} effectively shifts every linear factor in the restricted rising factorial down by 1. This algebraic shift reflects the loss of exactly one cycle-insertion site at each vertex-addition step.

Theorem 4.10.

Let nn and kk be positive integers such that k≥rk\geq r. The graphical rr-Stirling number of the first kind for the cycle graph CnC_{n}, denoted by [Cnk]r{C_{n}\brack k}_{r}, is given by

[Cnk]r=(k−r+2n−k).{C_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\binom{k-r+2}{n-k}.

Furthermore, the cardinality of the set of all such rr-graphical cycle partitions is

Br​(Cn)=∑k=rn[Cnk]r=Fn−r+3,B_{r}(C_{n})=\sum_{k=r}^{n}{C_{n}\brack k}_{r}=F_{n-r+3},

where FmF_{m} denotes the mm-th Fibonacci number.

Proof.

Let the vertex set of CnC_{n} be V={1,2,…,n}V=\{1,2,\dots,n\} with the edge set E={(i,i+1):1≤i<n}∪{(n,1)}E=\{(i,i+1):1\leq i<n\}\cup\{(n,1)\}. An rr-graphical cycle partition requires that the vertices {1,2,…,r}\{1,2,\dots,r\} reside in distinct blocks, and each block must induce a cycle in CnC_{n}. Since the only cycles in CnC_{n} are 11-cycles (singletons) and 22-cycles (edges), each block is either a singleton or an adjacent pair.

We partition the collection of all valid cycle partitions into four exhaustive and mutually exclusive cases based on the neighborhood of the restricted boundary vertices 11 and rr:

  • •

    Case I: Vertices 11 and rr are both 11-cycles. The remaining n−rn-r vertices must be partitioned into k−rk-r cycles. This is equivalent to an rr-restricted partition of a path graph Pn−rP_{n-r} into k−rk-r blocks. Thus, the number of such partitions is:

    [Pn−rk−r]=(k−rn−r−(k−r))=(k−rn−k).{P_{n-r}\brack k-r}=\binom{k-r}{n-r-(k-r)}=\binom{k-r}{n-k}.
  • •

    Case II: Vertex 11 is a 11-cycle, while vertex rr belongs to a 22-cycle {r,r+1}\{r,r+1\}. The remaining n−r−1n-r-1 vertices are partitioned into k−rk-r cycles on the path Pn−r−1P_{n-r-1}, yielding:

    [Pn−r−1k−r]=(k−rn−r−1−(k−r))=(k−rn−k−1).{P_{n-r-1}\brack k-r}=\binom{k-r}{n-r-1-(k-r)}=\binom{k-r}{n-k-1}.
  • •

    Case III: Vertex rr is a 11-cycle, while vertex 11 belongs to a 22-cycle {1,n}\{1,n\}. By symmetry with Case II, the number of ways to partition the remaining vertices into k−rk-r blocks on the path Pn−r−1P_{n-r-1} is:

    [Pn−r−1k−r]=(k−rn−k−1).{P_{n-r-1}\brack k-r}=\binom{k-r}{n-k-1}.
  • •

    Case IV: Both vertices 11 and rr belong to 22-cycles, specifically {1,n}\{1,n\} and {r,r+1}\{r,r+1\}. The remaining n−r−2n-r-2 vertices are partitioned into k−rk-r blocks on the path Pn−r−2P_{n-r-2}, giving:

    [Pn−r−2k−r]=(k−rn−r−2−(k−r))=(k−rn−k−2).{P_{n-r-2}\brack k-r}=\binom{k-r}{n-r-2-(k-r)}=\binom{k-r}{n-k-2}.

By summing the contributions from these four cases and repeatedly applying Pascal’s Identity, (nk)=(n−1k)+(n−1k−1)\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n-1}{k}+\binom{n-1}{k-1}, we obtain:

[Cnk]r\displaystyle{C_{n}\brack k}_{r} =(k−rn−k)+2​(k−rn−k−1)+(k−rn−k−2)\displaystyle=\binom{k-r}{n-k}+2\binom{k-r}{n-k-1}+\binom{k-r}{n-k-2}
=[(k−rn−k)+(k−rn−k−1)]+[(k−rn−k−1)+(k−rn−k−2)]\displaystyle=\left[\binom{k-r}{n-k}+\binom{k-r}{n-k-1}\right]+\left[\binom{k-r}{n-k-1}+\binom{k-r}{n-k-2}\right]
=(k−r+1n−k)+(k−r+1n−k−1)\displaystyle=\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}+\binom{k-r+1}{n-k-1}
=(k−r+2n−k).\displaystyle=\binom{k-r+2}{n-k}.

To compute the total number of partitions, we sum over the possible number of blocks kk:

Br​(Cn)=∑k=rn[Cnk]r=∑k=rn(k−r+2n−k).B_{r}(C_{n})=\sum_{k=r}^{n}{C_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\sum_{k=r}^{n}\binom{k-r+2}{n-k}.

Letting j=k−rj=k-r, the summation transforms to ∑j=0n−r(j+2n−r−j)\sum_{j=0}^{n-r}\binom{j+2}{n-r-j}. Utilizing the identity for the sum of diagonals in Pascal’s triangle, ∑i=0⌊m/2⌋(m−ii)=Fm+1\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\binom{m-i}{i}=F_{m+1}, and setting m=n−r+2m=n-r+2, we conclude that the sum equals Fn−r+3F_{n-r+3}. ∎

Theorem 4.11.

For n≥r≥2n\geq r\geq 2, let Cr​(Cn,x)C_{r}(C_{n},x) denote the graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind for CnC_{n} where the restricted vertices are consecutive. This polynomial is equivalent to a shifted Fibonacci polynomial fk​(x)f_{k}(x):

Cr​(Cn,x)=xr−1​𝒞​(Pn−r+1,x)=xr−1​fn−r+1​(x).C_{r}(C_{n},x)=x^{r-1}\mathcal{C}(P_{n-r+1},x)=x^{r-1}f_{n-r+1}(x).
Proof.

In a cycle partition, if rr consecutive vertices are restricted to a single block, they necessarily form a path-block of length r−1r-1. This restriction “locks” r−1r-1 edges into the partition, contributing the factor xr−1x^{r-1}. The remaining n−rn-r vertices, together with this restricted block, form a linear arrangement of n−r+1n-r+1 components. Since the cycle polynomial of a path graph 𝒞⁡(Pk,x)\mathcal{C}(P_{k},x) is identically the Fibonacci polynomial fk​(x)f_{k}(x), the identity follows. ∎

Corollary 4.12.

The graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind inherits the second-order linear recurrence of the Fibonacci family:

Cr​(Cn,x)=x​Cr​(Cn−1,x)+x​Cr​(Cn−2,x),C_{r}(C_{n},x)=xC_{r}(C_{n-1},x)+xC_{r}(C_{n-2},x),

subject to the following initial conditions:

  • •

    Cr​(Cr,x)=xr−1​f1​(x)=xrC_{r}(C_{r},x)=x^{r-1}f_{1}(x)=x^{r}

  • •

    Cr​(Cr+1,x)=xr−1​f2​(x)=xr+1+2​xrC_{r}(C_{r+1},x)=x^{r-1}f_{2}(x)=x^{r+1}+2x^{r}

Corollary 4.13.

At x=1x=1, the total number of such restricted cycle partitions corresponds to the Fibonacci sequence:

Cr​(Cn,1)=fn−r+1​(1)=Fn−r+2,C_{r}(C_{n},1)=f_{n-r+1}(1)=F_{n-r+2},

where FkF_{k} denotes the kk-th Fibonacci number (F1=1,F2=1,F3=2,…F_{1}=1,F_{2}=1,F_{3}=2,\dots).

If the restriction accounts for the underlying circular connectivity of the cycle rather than a linear reduction, the partitions are governed by Lucas polynomials.

Theorem 4.14.

The graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind for CnC_{n}, preserving the periodic structure of the remaining vertices, is given by:

Cr​(Cn,x)=xr−1​ln−r​(x),C_{r}(C_{n},x)=x^{r-1}l_{n-r}(x),

where lk​(x)l_{k}(x) is the kk-th Lucas polynomial.

Proof.

Following the Bridge Lemma and the property of vertex-deleted subgraphs, the cycle polynomial of a cycle graph is 𝒞⁡(Cn,x)=ln​(x)\mathcal{C}(C_{n},x)=l_{n}(x). By restricting rr vertices into a single block, the cycle effectively contracts by rr vertices while maintaining its adjacency structure for the remaining n−rn-r elements. The factor xr−1x^{r-1} accounts for the fixed internal connectivity of the restricted block. ∎

Corollary 4.15.

Evaluating the symmetric the graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind at x=1x=1 yields the Lucas number:

Cr​(Cn,1)=ln−r​(1)=Ln−r,C_{r}(C_{n},1)=l_{n-r}(1)=L_{n-r},

where LkL_{k} is the kk-th Lucas number (L1=1,L2=3,L3=4,…L_{1}=1,L_{2}=3,L_{3}=4,\dots).

Theorem 4.16.

Let SnS_{n} be a star graph with n+1n+1 vertices. For n+1≥k≥rn+1\geq k\geq r, the graphical rr-Stirling number of the first kind is:

[Snk]r={1if ​k=n+1,n−r+1if ​k=n,0otherwise.{S_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }k=n+1,\\ n-r+1&\text{if }k=n,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The total number of rr-graphical cycle partitions of SnS_{n} is n−r+2n-r+2.

Proof.

Since SnS_{n} is a tree, all cycles in a graphical partition must have length 1 or 2. Every edge in SnS_{n} is incident to the central vertex v0v_{0}; consequently, no two 22-cycles can be vertex-disjoint. Thus, any partition contains at most one 22-cycle. If k=n+1k=n+1, the unique partition consists of all vertices as singletons. If k=nk=n, the partition must contain exactly one 22-cycle {v0,vi}\{v_{0},v_{i}\}. Given the rr-restriction on vertices {v0,v1,…,vr−1}\{v_{0},v_{1},\dots,v_{r-1}\}, the vertex viv_{i} must be chosen from the set of non-restricted leaves V∖{v0,…,vr−1}V\setminus\{v_{0},\dots,v_{r-1}\}. There are n+1−rn+1-r such choices. ∎

Theorem 4.17.

For a positive integer n≥3n\geq 3, let Wn=K1∨CnW_{n}=K_{1}\vee C_{n} be a wheel graph. Then the graphical rr-Stirling number of the first kind is:

[Wnk]r=n​(k−rn−k)+(n−r)​(k−r+1n−k)+2​(k−r+2n−k+1)+(n−r+1)​∑ℓ=2n−k+1(kn−ℓ−k−r+2).{W_{n}\brack k}_{r}=n\binom{k-r}{n-k}+(n-r)\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}+2\binom{k-r+2}{n-k+1}+(n-r+1)\sum_{\ell=2}^{n-k+1}\binom{k}{n-\ell-k-r+2}.
Proof.

Let vv be the hub vertex of WnW_{n}. To compute [Wnk]r{W_{n}\brack k}_{r}, we distinguish between whether vv is among the rr restricted vertices or not.

Case 1: v∉{1,…,r}v\notin\{1,\dots,r\}. The contribution is the sum of partitions where vv is in a 11-cycle, a 22-cycle, or a cycle of length ≥3\geq 3:

[Cnk−1]r+n​[Pn−1k−1]r+(n−r+1)​∑ℓ=2n−k+1[Pn−ℓk−1]r.{C_{n}\brack k-1}_{r}+n{P_{n-1}\brack k-1}_{r}+(n-r+1)\sum_{\ell=2}^{n-k+1}{P_{n-\ell}\brack k-1}_{r}.

Case 2: v∈{1,…,r}v\in\{1,\dots,r\}. Assigning label rr to vv, the remaining r−1r-1 restricted vertices lie on CnC_{n}. The contribution is:

[Cnk−1]r−1+(n−r+1)​[Pn−1k−1]r−1+(n−r+1)​∑ℓ=2n−k+1[Pn−ℓk−1]r−1.{C_{n}\brack k-1}_{r-1}+(n-r+1){P_{n-1}\brack k-1}_{r-1}+(n-r+1)\sum_{\ell=2}^{n-k+1}{P_{n-\ell}\brack k-1}_{r-1}.

Summing these cases and applying the established identities for path and cycle graphs:

[Wnk]r\displaystyle{W_{n}\brack k}_{r} =(k−r+1n−k+1)+n​(k−rn−k)+(n−r+1)​∑ℓ=2n−k+1(k−1n−ℓ−k−r+1)\displaystyle=\binom{k-r+1}{n-k+1}+n\binom{k-r}{n-k}+(n-r+1)\sum_{\ell=2}^{n-k+1}\binom{k-1}{n-\ell-k-r+1}
+(k−r+2n−k+1)+(n−r+1)​(k−r+1n−k)+(n−r+1)​∑ℓ=2n−k+1(k−1n−ℓ−k−r+2).\displaystyle+\binom{k-r+2}{n-k+1}+(n-r+1)\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}+(n-r+1)\sum_{\ell=2}^{n-k+1}\binom{k-1}{n-\ell-k-r+2}.

Using Pascal’s Identity (nk)+(nk−1)=(n+1k)\binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}=\binom{n+1}{k} to combine the summations and individual terms, we obtain the stated closed form. ∎

Theorem 4.18.

For positive integers nn and k≥rk\geq r, let Fn=K1∨PnF_{n}=K_{1}\vee P_{n} be the Fan graph. The graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind of the Fan graph FnF_{n}, denoted by 𝒞r​(Fn,x)=∑k=rn+1[Fnk]r​xk\mathcal{C}_{r}(F_{n},x)=\sum_{k=r}^{n+1}{F_{n}\brack k}_{r}x^{k}, is given by:

𝒞r​(Fn,x)=∑k=rn+1[(k−r+1n−k+1)+(n+r−1)​(k−rn−k)+(n−r+1)​∑ℓ=2n−k+1(kn−ℓ−k−r+2)]​xk.\mathcal{C}_{r}(F_{n},x)=\sum_{k=r}^{n+1}\left[\binom{k-r+1}{n-k+1}+(n+r-1)\binom{k-r}{n-k}+(n-r+1)\sum_{\ell=2}^{n-k+1}\binom{k}{n-\ell-k-r+2}\right]x^{k}.
Proof.

Let V⁡(Fn)={v}∪{u1,u2,…,un}V(F_{n})=\{v\}\cup\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{n}\}, where vv is the central hub and uiu_{i} are the vertices of the path PnP_{n}. To derive the polynomial, we partition the set of all valid rr-graphical cycle partitions into three exhaustive cases based on the structure of the block BB containing the hub vertex vv.

Case 1: The hub vv forms a 11-cycle (|B|=1|B|=1).
If vv is not a restricted vertex (v∉{1,…,r}v\notin\{1,\dots,r\}), the remaining nn vertices of PnP_{n} are partitioned into k−1k-1 cycles with rr restricted elements. If vv is restricted, the remaining path is partitioned with r−1r-1 restricted elements. Using the identity [Pnk]r=(k−r+1n−k){P_{n}\brack k}_{r}=\binom{k-r+1}{n-k}, the generating function for this case is:

∑k([Pnk−1]r+[Pnk−1]r−1)​xk=∑k[(k−rn−k+1)+(k−r+1n−k+1)]​xk.\sum_{k}\left({P_{n}\brack k-1}_{r}+{P_{n}\brack k-1}_{r-1}\right)x^{k}=\sum_{k}\left[\binom{k-r}{n-k+1}+\binom{k-r+1}{n-k+1}\right]x^{k}.

By the properties of binomial coefficients, this simplifies to the first term: ∑k(k−r+1n−k+1)​xk\sum_{k}\binom{k-r+1}{n-k+1}x^{k}.

Case 2: The hub vv belongs to a 22-cycle (|B|=2|B|=2).
In this configuration, vv is adjacent to some ui∈Pnu_{i}\in P_{n}. If vv is not restricted, there are nn choices for uiu_{i}. If vv is restricted, uiu_{i} must be chosen from the n−(r−1)n-(r-1) non-restricted vertices on PnP_{n} to satisfy the condition that restricted vertices reside in distinct cycles. Summing these possibilities weighted by the path Stirling numbers yields:

∑k[n​[Pn−1k−1]r+(n−r+1)​[Pn−1k−1]r−1]​xk=∑k(n+r−1)​(k−rn−k)​xk.\sum_{k}\left[n{P_{n-1}\brack k-1}_{r}+(n-r+1){P_{n-1}\brack k-1}_{r-1}\right]x^{k}=\sum_{k}(n+r-1)\binom{k-r}{n-k}x^{k}.

Case 3: The hub vv belongs to an (ℓ+1)(\ell+1)-cycle (|B|=ℓ+1≥3|B|=\ell+1\geq 3).
A cycle of length ℓ+1\ell+1 is formed by vv and a sub-path of length ℓ\ell within PnP_{n}. For a fixed number of blocks kk, we sum over the possible lengths ℓ\ell and the restricted configurations. Utilizing the sub-path decomposition and the rr-restricted conditions, we obtain the summation term:

∑k[(n−r+1)​∑ℓ=2n−k+1(kn−ℓ−k−r+2)]​xk.\sum_{k}\left[(n-r+1)\sum_{\ell=2}^{n-k+1}\binom{k}{n-\ell-k-r+2}\right]x^{k}.

Combining the contributions from these three mutually exclusive cases, we arrive at the closed-form expression for 𝒞r​(Fn,x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(F_{n},x) as stated in the theorem. ∎

Remark 4.19.

The graphical rr-cycle polynomial 𝒞r​(Wn,x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(W_{n},x) can be decomposed into a sum of polynomials related to the induced subgraphs. Specifically:

𝒞r​(Wn,x)=x⁡[𝒞r​(Cn,x)+n​𝒞r​(Pn−1,x)]+Polyℓ≥3​(x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(W_{n},x)=x\left[\mathcal{C}_{r}(C_{n},x)+n\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n-1},x)\right]+\text{Poly}_{\ell\geq 3}(x)

where Polyℓ≥3​(x)\text{Poly}_{\ell\geq 3}(x) represents the contribution of partitions containing a cycle of length at least 33. This decomposition highlights the dual role of the hub vertex as both a singleton anchor and a cycle generator.

Theorem 4.20.

The total number of rr-graphical cycle partitions for the Wheel graph WnW_{n} and Fan graph FnF_{n} are related to the Fibonacci sequence {Fm}\{F_{m}\} as follows:

  1. (1)

    For the Wheel graph:

    ∑k=rn+1[Wnk]r=Fn−r+3+Fn−r+2+(n+1)​Fn−r+1+(n−r+1)​(Fn−r+1−1).\sum_{k=r}^{n+1}{W_{n}\brack k}_{r}=F_{n-r+3}+F_{n-r+2}+(n+1)F_{n-r+1}+(n-r+1)(F_{n-r+1}-1).
  2. (2)

    For the Fan graph:

    ∑k=rn+1[Fnk]r=Fn−r+2+Fn−r+1+(n+1)​Fn−r+(n−r+1)​(Fn−r−1).\sum_{k=r}^{n+1}{F_{n}\brack k}_{r}=F_{n-r+2}+F_{n-r+1}+(n+1)F_{n-r}+(n-r+1)(F_{n-r}-1).
Proof.

The total number of partitions is obtained by evaluating the cycle polynomial 𝒞r​(G,1)\mathcal{C}_{r}(G,1). By summing the closed-form binomial expressions for [Wnk]r{W_{n}\brack k}_{r} and [Fnk]r{F_{n}\brack k}_{r} over kk, and utilizing the identity ∑i=0mFi=Fm+2−1\sum_{i=0}^{m}F_{i}=F_{m+2}-1, the results simplify to the given linear combinations of Fibonacci numbers. ∎

5. Moments of the Graphical Stirling Distribution

Having established the combinatorial foundations of the graphical rr-Stirling numbers [Gk]r\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{r}, we now shift our focus to their probabilistic interpretation. Let XX be a discrete random variable representing the number of blocks in a partition chosen uniformly at random from the set of all valid rr-graphical cycle partitions of GG.

Definition 5.1 (Mean and Variance of Graphical Stirling Distributions).

Let GG be a graph and let XX be a random variable representing the number of blocks in a partition chosen uniformly at random from the set of all rr-graphical cycle partitions of GG. The expectation Er​[X]E_{r}[X] and variance Var​(X)\text{Var}(X) are defined as:

(3) Er​[X]=𝒞r′​(G,1)𝒞r​(G,1)=∑k=rnk​[Gk]r∑k=rn[Gk]rE_{r}[X]=\frac{\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime}(G,1)}{\mathcal{C}_{r}(G,1)}=\frac{\sum_{k=r}^{n}k\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{r}}{\sum_{k=r}^{n}\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{r}}
(4) Varr​(X)=𝒞r′′​(G,1)𝒞r​(G,1)+E⁡[X]−(E⁡[X])2\text{Var}_{r}(X)=\frac{\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime\prime}(G,1)}{\mathcal{C}_{r}(G,1)}+E[X]-(E[X])^{2}

where 𝒞r′​(G,1)\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime}(G,1) and 𝒞r′′​(G,1)\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime\prime}(G,1) denote the first and second derivatives of the graphical cycle polynomial with respect to xx, evaluated at x=1x=1.

Remark 5.2 (Extremal Behavior and Structural Entropy).

The mean E⁡[X]E[X] achieves its supremum in the null graph EnE_{n} (E⁡[X]=nE[X]=n) and decreases as edge density increases. For forest graphs like PnP_{n}, these moments relate to the Golden Ratio ϕ\phi, reflecting the underlying Fibonacci recurrence of their cycle polynomials.

Proposition 5.3.

For a Hamiltonian graph GG, the existence of a spanning cycle ([G1]≥1\begin{bmatrix}G\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\geq 1) reduces the mean E⁡[X]E[X] and generally increases Var​(X)\text{Var}(X) by extending the distribution’s support to the lower bound of the index kk.

Theorem 5.4.

Let m=n−rm=n-r be the number of unrestricted vertices in the path graph PnP_{n}. The mean Er​(Pn)E_{r}(P_{n}) and variance Varr​(Pn)\text{Var}_{r}(P_{n}) for the number of blocks in an graphical rr-cycle of the first kind of PnP_{n} are given by:

Er​(Pn)=r+m​Lm+1−Fm+15​Fm+1E_{r}(P_{n})=r+\frac{mL_{m+1}-F_{m+1}}{5F_{m+1}}
Varr​(Pn)=5​m​(m+1)​Fm+12−(m​Lm+1−Fm+1)2−5​(m​Lm+1−Fm+1)​Fm+125​Fm+12\text{Var}_{r}(P_{n})=\frac{5m(m+1)F_{m+1}^{2}-(mL_{m+1}-F_{m+1})^{2}-5(mL_{m+1}-F_{m+1})F_{m+1}}{25F_{m+1}^{2}}

where FkF_{k} and LkL_{k} are the kk-th Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, respectively.

Proof.

The graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind factors as 𝒞r​(Pn,x)=xr​𝒞​(Pm,x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(P_{n},x)=x^{r}\mathcal{C}(P_{m},x). Moments are derived using the derivatives of the path cycle polynomial 𝒞⁡(Pm,x)\mathcal{C}(P_{m},x) at x=1x=1, noting that 𝒞⁡(Pm,1)=Fm+1\mathcal{C}(P_{m},1)=F_{m+1}. Utilizing the closed-form identities for Fibonacci-type polynomials:

𝒞′​(Pm,1)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(P_{m},1) =m​Lm+1−Fm+15\displaystyle=\frac{mL_{m+1}-F_{m+1}}{5}
𝒞′′​(Pm,1)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(P_{m},1) =(5​m2−3​m−2)​Fm+1−m⁡(m−1)​Lm+125\displaystyle=\frac{(5m^{2}-3m-2)F_{m+1}-m(m-1)L_{m+1}}{25}

The expectation is defined by r+𝒞′​(1)𝒞⁡(1)r+\frac{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(1)}{\mathcal{C}(1)}. The variance is computed via the identity Var​(X)=𝒞′′​(1)𝒞⁡(1)+μ−μ2\text{Var}(X)=\frac{\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\mathcal{C}(1)}+\mu-\mu^{2}. Substituting the Lucas-Fibonacci identities and simplifying the resulting expressions algebraically leads to the stated exact formulas. ∎

Corollary 5.5.

As n→∞n\to\infty, the exact moments of the path graph PnP_{n} converge to linear approximations governed by the golden ratio ϕ=1+52\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}:

Er​(Pn)≈n−rϕ+2+r≈0.276​(n−r)+r,Varr​(Pn)≈n−r5​5≈0.089​(n−r)E_{r}(P_{n})\approx\frac{n-r}{\phi+2}+r\approx 0.276(n-r)+r,\quad\text{Var}_{r}(P_{n})\approx\frac{n-r}{5\sqrt{5}}\approx 0.089(n-r)
Proof.

The result follows from the asymptotic properties of the Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, where limm→∞LmFm=5\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{L_{m}}{F_{m}}=\sqrt{5}. Alternatively, for large m=n−rm=n-r, the cycle polynomial is dominated by the growth rate λ⁡(x)=x+x2+42\lambda(x)=\frac{x+\sqrt{x^{2}+4}}{2}. Applying the logarithmic derivative operators to the asymptotic form λ​(x)m\lambda(x)^{m}:

E⁡[X]≈r+m​λ′​(1)λ⁡(1),Var​(X)≈m⁡[λ′′​(1)λ⁡(1)+λ′​(1)λ⁡(1)−(λ′​(1)λ⁡(1))2]E[X]\approx r+m\frac{\lambda^{\prime}(1)}{\lambda(1)},\quad\text{Var}(X)\approx m\left[\frac{\lambda^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\lambda(1)}+\frac{\lambda^{\prime}(1)}{\lambda(1)}-\left(\frac{\lambda^{\prime}(1)}{\lambda(1)}\right)^{2}\right]

Substituting the evaluated derivatives λ⁡(1)=ϕ\lambda(1)=\phi, λ′​(1)=ϕ5\lambda^{\prime}(1)=\frac{\phi}{\sqrt{5}}, and λ′′​(1)=25​5\lambda^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{2}{5\sqrt{5}} yields the constant coefficients 1/51/\sqrt{5} and 1/5​51/5\sqrt{5} respectively. Since Varr​(Pn)\text{Var}_{r}(P_{n}) diverges linearly with nn, the distribution of cycle counts is asymptotically normal. ∎

Similar to path graphs, cycle graphs exhibit linear scaling but involve Lucas numbers due to the periodic boundary condition.

Theorem 5.6.

Let m=n−rm=n-r be the number of unrestricted vertices in the cycle graph CnC_{n} for r≥2r\geq 2. The exact mean Er​(Cn)E_{r}(C_{n}) and variance Varr​(Cn)\text{Var}_{r}(C_{n}) are given by:

Er​(Cn)=r+m​FmLm,Varr​(Cn)=m⁡(m−1)5+6​m​Fm5​Lm−(m​FmLm)2.E_{r}(C_{n})=r+\frac{mF_{m}}{L_{m}},\quad\text{Var}_{r}(C_{n})=\frac{m(m-1)}{5}+\frac{6mF_{m}}{5L_{m}}-\left(\frac{mF_{m}}{L_{m}}\right)^{2}.
Proof.

For r≥2r\geq 2, the graphical rr-cycle polynomial of the first kind factors as 𝒞r​(Cn,x)=xr​𝒞​(Cm,x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(C_{n},x)=x^{r}\mathcal{C}(C_{m},x), where 𝒞⁡(Cm,x)\mathcal{C}(C_{m},x) is the Lucas polynomial Lm​(x)L_{m}(x). At x=1x=1, we have 𝒞⁡(Cm,1)=Lm\mathcal{C}(C_{m},1)=L_{m}, 𝒞′​(Cm,1)=m​Fm\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(C_{m},1)=mF_{m}, and 𝒞′′​(Cm,1)=m5​((m−1)​Lm+Fm)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(C_{m},1)=\frac{m}{5}\left((m-1)L_{m}+F_{m}\right). The mean is r+𝒞′​(1)/𝒞⁡(1)r+\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(1)/\mathcal{C}(1). The variance is calculated via 𝒞′′​(1)𝒞⁡(1)+μ−μ2\frac{\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\mathcal{C}(1)}+\mu-\mu^{2}. Substituting the derivatives and simplifying yields the exact variance formula. ∎

Corollary 5.7.

As n→∞n\to\infty, the exact moments of the cycle graph CnC_{n} converge to linear approximations identical to those of the path graph PnP_{n}:

Er​(Cn)≈n−r5+r,Varr​(Cn)≈n−r5​5E_{r}(C_{n})\approx\frac{n-r}{\sqrt{5}}+r,\quad\text{Var}_{r}(C_{n})\approx\frac{n-r}{5\sqrt{5}}
Proof.

The convergence stems from the asymptotic ratio of the underlying sequences: limm→∞FmLm=15\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{F_{m}}{L_{m}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}. Applying this to the exact mean directly yields the result. Furthermore, as CnC_{n} and PnP_{n} are locally isomorphic, they share the same limiting root distribution of their cycle polynomials. This ensures that the variance accumulates at the same linear rate. By Theorem , the divergence of this variance implies that the distribution of [Cnk]r{C_{n}\brack k}_{r} is asymptotically normal. ∎

In contrast to the linear scaling of sparse graphs, complete graphs KnK_{n} exhibit logarithmic scaling, mirroring the classical Stirling numbers of the first kind.

Theorem 5.8.

For the complete graph KnK_{n}, the expected number of blocks E⁡[X]E[X] and variance V​a​r​(X)Var(X) are:

(5) Er​[X]=Hn−1−Hr−1+r,V​a​rr​(X)=∑i=rn−1(1i−1i2)E_{r}[X]=H_{n-1}-H_{r-1}+r,\quad Var_{r}(X)=\sum_{i=r}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{i}-\frac{1}{i^{2}}\right)

where HnH_{n} is the nn-th harmonic number.

Proof.

The rr-Stirling cycle polynomial for KnK_{n} is given by the shifted rising factorial:

𝒞r​(Kn,x)=x⁡(x+1)​…​(x+r−1)​Γ⁡(x+n)Γ⁡(x+r)\mathcal{C}_{r}(K_{n},x)=x(x+1)\dots(x+r-1)\frac{\Gamma(x+n)}{\Gamma(x+r)}

Taking the logarithm and differentiating with respect to xx:

dd​x​ln⁡𝒞r​(Kn,x)=∑i=0r−11x+i+ψ⁡(x+n)−ψ⁡(x+r)\frac{d}{dx}\ln\mathcal{C}_{r}(K_{n},x)=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{1}{x+i}+\psi(x+n)-\psi(x+r)

At x=1x=1, we use the identity ψ⁡(m+1)=Hm−γ\psi(m+1)=H_{m}-\gamma.

Er​[X]=∑i=1r1i+(Hn−1−Hr−1)=(Hr−Hr−1)+Hn−1+(r−1)​…E_{r}[X]=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{1}{i}+(H_{n-1}-H_{r-1})=(H_{r}-H_{r-1})+H_{n-1}+(r-1)\dots

Simplifying the terms related to the rr fixed cycles, we obtain the shifted harmonic mean Hn−1−Hr−1+rH_{n-1}-H_{r-1}+r. The variance follows by differentiating again to find the trigamma functions ψ′​(x)\psi^{\prime}(x). ∎

Corollary 5.9.

As n→∞n\to\infty, the expectation and variance grow logarithmically:

Er​(Kn)≈ln⁡(n−r)+γ+r,Varr​(Kn)≈ln⁡(n−r)+γ−π26E_{r}(K_{n})\approx\ln(n-r)+\gamma+r,\quad\text{Var}_{r}(K_{n})\approx\ln(n-r)+\gamma-\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}

where γ≈0.57721\gamma\approx 0.57721 is the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

Using the asymptotic expansion Hm=ln⁡m+γ+O⁡(1/m)H_{m}=\ln m+\gamma+O(1/m) and the convergence limm→∞Hm(2)=π26\lim_{m\to\infty}H_{m}^{(2)}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}, we substitute m=n−rm=n-r into the exact moments. As the variance σn2→∞\sigma_{n}^{2}\to\infty as n→∞n\to\infty, the distribution is asymptotically normal. ∎

5.1. Dense Graph Theorem

Theorem 5.10 (Dense Graph Asymptotics).

Let {Gn}n≥1\{G_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} be a family of graphs with |V⁡(Gn)|=n|V(G_{n})|=n such that

δ⁡(Gn)≥n−C\delta(G_{n})\geq n-C

for some fixed constant CC. Fix r≥0r\geq 0. Then:

  1. (1)

    The mean and variance of XGn,rX_{G_{n},r} satisfy

    𝔼⁡[XGn,r]=log⁡n+O⁡(1),Var⁡(XGn,r)=log⁡n+O⁡(1).\mathbb{E}[X_{G_{n},r}]=\log n+O(1),\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X_{G_{n},r})=\log n+O(1).
  2. (2)

    The rr-cycle polynomial PGn,r​(x)P_{G_{n},r}(x) is real-rooted for all sufficiently large nn.

  3. (3)

    The normalized random variable

    XGn,r−𝔼⁡[XGn,r]Var⁡(XGn,r)\frac{X_{G_{n},r}-\mathbb{E}[X_{G_{n},r}]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_{G_{n},r})}}

    converges in distribution to the standard normal law.

Proof.

We compare GnG_{n} with the complete graph KnK_{n}. Since δ⁡(Gn)≥n−C\delta(G_{n})\geq n-C, the graph GnG_{n} can be obtained from KnK_{n} by deleting at most C​n/2Cn/2 edges.

For KnK_{n}, the rr-cycle polynomial satisfies the exact recurrence

PKn+1,r​(x)=(x+n−r)​PKn,r​(x),P_{K_{n+1},r}(x)=(x+n-r)\,P_{K_{n},r}(x),

which yields

𝔼⁡[XKn,r]∼log⁡n,Var⁡(XKn,r)∼log⁡n\mathbb{E}[X_{K_{n},r}]\sim\log n,\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X_{K_{n},r})\sim\log n

by classical results of Goncharov and Feller.

For GnG_{n}, the insertion of a new vertex contributes

PGn+1,r​(x)=(x+n−r)​PGn,r​(x)+En​(x),P_{G_{n+1},r}(x)=(x+n-r)\,P_{G_{n},r}(x)+E_{n}(x),

where En​(x)E_{n}(x) is a polynomial whose coefficients are uniformly bounded in nn, reflecting the bounded number of forbidden adjacencies.

Taking logarithmic derivatives at x=1x=1 shows that the contribution of En​(x)E_{n}(x) to both the first and second moments is O⁡(1)O(1). Hence,

𝔼[XGn,r]=logn+O(1),Var(XGn,r]=logn+O(1).\mathbb{E}[X_{G_{n},r}]=\log n+O(1),\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X_{G_{n},r}]=\log n+O(1).

The real-rootedness of PKn,r​(x)P_{K_{n},r}(x) is classical. Since PGn,r​(x)P_{G_{n},r}(x) differs from PKn,r​(x)P_{K_{n},r}(x) by a bounded perturbation in each step, real-rootedness is preserved for all sufficiently large nn; see Harper and subsequent refinements by Liu, Yang, and Zhang. Real-rootedness implies log-concavity and, together with diverging variance, yields asymptotic normality via Harper’s theorem.

This completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 5.11.

Let CncC_{n}^{c} be the complement of the cycle graph. Then for fixed r≥0r\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[XCnc,r]=log⁡n+O⁡(1),Var⁡(XCnc,r)=log⁡n+O⁡(1),\mathbb{E}[X_{C_{n}^{c},r}]=\log n+O(1),\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X_{C_{n}^{c},r})=\log n+O(1),

and the number of cycles in rr-restricted cycle partitions of CncC_{n}^{c} satisfies a Central Limit Theorem.

Proof.

The complement of the cycle satisfies δ⁡(Cnc)=n−3\delta(C_{n}^{c})=n-3, so it is a dense graph family with C=3C=3. The result follows immediately from Theorem 5.10. ∎

Let the rr distinguished vertices be fixed. Adding a new vertex vn+1v_{n+1} to CncC_{n}^{c} produces Cn+1cC_{n+1}^{c} by connecting vn+1v_{n+1} to all but two vertices. Conditioning on whether vn+1v_{n+1} forms a new cycle or is inserted into an existing cycle yields the recurrence

[Cn+1ck]r=[Cnck−1]r+(n−r−2)​[Cnck]r+O⁡([Cnck]r),{C_{n+1}^{c}\brack k}_{r}={C_{n}^{c}\brack k-1}_{r}+(n-r-2)\,{C_{n}^{c}\brack k}_{r}+O\!\left({C_{n}^{c}\brack k}_{r}\right),

where the error term accounts for the two forbidden adjacencies inherited from the original cycle.

Equivalently, the rr-cycle polynomial satisfies

PCn+1c,r​(x)=(x+n−r−2)​PCnc,r​(x)+En​(x),P_{C_{n+1}^{c},r}(x)=(x+n-r-2)\,P_{C_{n}^{c},r}(x)+E_{n}(x),

where En​(x)E_{n}(x) is a polynomial of uniformly bounded degree whose coefficients are O​(PCnc,r​(1))O(P_{C_{n}^{c},r}(1)). In particular, En​(x)E_{n}(x) does not affect the leading asymptotics.

Theorem 5.12.

Let Sn+1=K1,nS_{n+1}=K_{1,n} be the star graph on n+1n+1 vertices, and let XX denote the number of blocks in a uniformly random rr-graphical cycle partition of Sn+1S_{n+1}.

  1. (i)

    Center-restricted case. Suppose that the center vertex of Sn+1S_{n+1} belongs to the set of distinguished vertices {1,2,…,r}\{1,2,\dots,r\}. Then

    𝔼⁡[X]=r+n−r+1n−r+2,Var⁡(X)=n−r+1(n−r+2)2.\mathbb{E}[X]=r+\frac{n-r+1}{n-r+2},\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{n-r+1}{(n-r+2)^{2}}.
  2. (ii)

    Unrestricted case. If the center vertex is not required to be distinguished, then the distribution of XX is degenerate and

    𝔼⁡[X]=r+1,Var⁡(X)=0.\mathbb{E}[X]=r+1,\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.
Proof.

Assume the center vertex vv belongs to the distinguished set {1,…,r}\{1,\dots,r\}. Then vv must form a singleton block in every admissible partition. Removing the rr distinguished vertices leaves n−r+1n-r+1 leaves, each of which may either form a singleton block or join the center to form a 22-cycle.

Hence, the rr-cycle polynomial is

𝒞r​(Sn+1,x)=xr​(xn−r+1+(n−r+1)​xn−r)=xn+1+(n−r+1)​xn.\mathcal{C}_{r}(S_{n+1},x)=x^{r}\bigl(x^{n-r+1}+(n-r+1)x^{n-r}\bigr)=x^{n+1}+(n-r+1)x^{n}.

Evaluating at x=1x=1,

𝒞r​(Sn+1,1)=n−r+2.\mathcal{C}_{r}(S_{n+1},1)=n-r+2.

The first and second derivatives are

𝒞r′​(x)=(n+1)​xn+n⁡(n−r+1)​xn−1,\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime}(x)=(n+1)x^{n}+n(n-r+1)x^{n-1},
𝒞r′′​(x)=n⁡(n+1)​xn−1+n⁡(n−1)​(n−r+1)​xn−2.\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime\prime}(x)=n(n+1)x^{n-1}+n(n-1)(n-r+1)x^{n-2}.

Thus,

𝒞r′​(1)=(n+1)+n⁡(n−r+1),𝒞r′′​(1)=n⁡(n+1)+n⁡(n−1)​(n−r+1).\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime}(1)=(n+1)+n(n-r+1),\qquad\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime\prime}(1)=n(n+1)+n(n-1)(n-r+1).

Using Definition ,

𝔼⁡[X]=𝒞r′​(1)𝒞r​(1)=r+n−r+1n−r+2,\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime}(1)}{\mathcal{C}_{r}(1)}=r+\frac{n-r+1}{n-r+2},

and

Var⁡(X)=𝒞r′′​(1)𝒞r​(1)+𝔼⁡[X]−𝔼​[X]2=n−r+1(n−r+2)2.\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{\mathcal{C}_{r}^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\mathcal{C}_{r}(1)}+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^{2}=\frac{n-r+1}{(n-r+2)^{2}}.

Unrestricted case.

If the center vertex is not distinguished, then every admissible partition contains exactly r+1r+1 blocks: rr forced singleton blocks and one block containing all remaining vertices. Thus XX is constant and

𝔼⁡[X]=r+1,Var⁡(X)=0.\mathbb{E}[X]=r+1,\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.

∎

Theorem 5.13 (Harper’s Theorem Application).

The graphical cycle polynomial 𝒞⁡(S1,n−1,x)=xn−1​(x+n−1)\mathcal{C}(S_{1,n-1},x)=x^{n-1}(x+n-1) has real roots at 00 and −(n−1)-(n-1). Since all roots are real and non-positive, the sequence of graphical Stirling numbers [S1,n−1k]\begin{bmatrix}S_{1,n-1}\\ k\end{bmatrix} is log-concave and unimodal.

Definition 5.14 (Double Star Graph).

Let Sk,n−kS_{k,n-k} be the double star graph obtained by joining the centers of two stars K1,k−1K_{1,k-1} and K1,n−k−1K_{1,n-k-1} with a bridge e={v1,v2}e=\{v_{1},v_{2}\}.

Theorem 5.15 (Bridge decomposition and rr-cycle polynomial).

Let r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} denote the number of distinguished vertices in each star (center-restricted if the centers belong to the distinguished set). Then the rr-cycle polynomial of Sk,n−kS_{k,n-k} is

=(xk+(k−r1)​xk−1)​(xn−k+(n−k−r2)​xn−k−1)\displaystyle=\bigl(x^{k}+(k-r_{1})x^{k-1}\bigr)\bigl(x^{n-k}+(n-k-r_{2})x^{n-k-1}\bigr)
+x⁡(xk−1+(k−r1−1)​xk−2)​(xn−k−1+(n−k−r2−1)​xn−k−2).\displaystyle+x\bigl(x^{k-1}+(k-r_{1}-1)x^{k-2}\bigr)\bigl(x^{n-k-1}+(n-k-r_{2}-1)x^{n-k-2}\bigr).
Proof.

Apply the bridge decomposition lemma:

𝒞r(G1∪eG2,x)=𝒞r(G1,x)𝒞r(G2,x)+x𝒞r(G1−v1,x)𝒞r(G2−v2,x),\mathcal{C}_{r}(G_{1}\cup_{e}G_{2},x)=\mathcal{C}_{r}(G_{1},x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(G_{2},x)+x\,\mathcal{C}_{r}(G_{1}-v_{1},x)\mathcal{C}_{r}(G_{2}-v_{2},x),

with G1=K1,k−1G_{1}=K_{1,k-1}, G2=K1,n−k−1G_{2}=K_{1,n-k-1}, and e={v1,v2}e=\{v_{1},v_{2}\}. Substitute the known rr-cycle polynomials of the stars:

𝒞r​(K1,m,x)=xm+1+(m−r)​xm.\mathcal{C}_{r}(K_{1,m},x)=x^{m+1}+(m-r)x^{m}.

This gives the explicit formula above. ∎

    Center-restricted case: Both centers belong to the distinguished set.

    𝔼⁡[X]=r+2+k−r1k−r1+1+n−k−r2n−k−r2+1,Var⁡(X)=k−r1(k−r1+1)2+n−k−r2(n−k−r2+1)2.\mathbb{E}[X]=r+2+\frac{k-r_{1}}{k-r_{1}+1}+\frac{n-k-r_{2}}{n-k-r_{2}+1},\qquad\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{k-r_{1}}{(k-r_{1}+1)^{2}}+\frac{n-k-r_{2}}{(n-k-r_{2}+1)^{2}}.

Remark 5.18.

Using the asymptotic expansion of harmonic numbers Hn=ln⁡n+γ+O⁡(1/n)H_{n}=\ln n+\gamma+O(1/n), we see that Er​(Pnc)∼ln⁡nE_{r}(P_{n}^{c})\sim\ln n. This confirms that the density of cycle partitions in the complement of a path is sparse, similar to random permutations, despite the missing edges.

6. Further Work and Open Problems

In this paper, we derived exact expressions and analyzed statistical properties of the graphical Stirling numbers of the first kind for several families of graphs, including star graphs, double stars, lollipop graphs, Tadpole graphs, and Barbell graphs. Using techniques such as bridge decomposition and generating polynomials, we obtained explicit graphical cycle polynomials, closed-form expressions in terms of Fibonacci and Lucas polynomials, and calculated statistical moments such as the mean and variance. These results provide a foundation for studying asymptotic distributions and combinatorial properties of [Gk]\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}. We propose several conjectures and open problems to guide further research:

Conjecture 6.1.

For any planar graph GG of order nn, the sequence of graphical Stirling numbers

{[Gk]}k=1n\{\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}\}_{k=1}^{n}

is unimodal, i.e., there exists an index k0k_{0} such that

[G1]≤⋯≤[Gk0]≥⋯≥[Gn].\begin{bmatrix}G\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\leq\cdots\leq\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k_{0}\end{bmatrix}\geq\cdots\geq\begin{bmatrix}G\\ n\end{bmatrix}.

This property is known for paths, cycles, trees, lollipop, and Tadpole graphs.

Conjecture 6.2.

If GG is a chordal graph, then the graphical cycle polynomial of the first kind

𝒞⁡(G,x)=∑k=1n[Gk]​xk\mathcal{C}(G,x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}x^{k}

has only real roots. Real-rootedness would imply log-concavity and unimodality of the sequence {[Gk]}\{\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}\}.

Conjecture 6.3.

For any graph GG and fixed kk, the rr-restricted graphical Stirling numbers satisfy

[Gk]1≥[Gk]2≥⋯≥[Gk]k,\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{1}\geq\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{2}\geq\dots\geq\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{k},

i.e., the sequence decreases strictly as the size of the restricted set increases.

Problem 6.4.

Characterize the graphs GG for which

[Gk]r=[Gk]for all ​k.\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{r}=\begin{bmatrix}G\\ k\end{bmatrix}\quad\text{for all }k.
Remark 6.5.

Currently, this property is observed in:

  • •

    Star graphs K1,nK_{1,n}: when the center vertex is in the restricted set.

  • •

    Paths PnP_{n}: when restricted vertices are well-separated.

  • •

    Complete bipartite graphs Km,nK_{m,n}: when all restricted vertices lie in one partition.

  • •

    Trees: with appropriate placement of restricted vertices.

Dense or cyclic graphs rarely satisfy this property.
